text: Telehealth visit. 47-year-old male presents with two months of low energy, poor sleep, loss of interest in work and hobbies, and occasional tearfulness. He also reports easy fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Labs ordered last week showed hemoglobin 9.8 with low MCHC; iron studies pending; no obvious bleeding source. PHQ-9 score 18 consistent with a single episode of major depression, moderate severity. Started sertraline 50 mg daily and iron supplementation. Plan: repeat CBC in 4 weeks, follow up in 2 weeks to assess mood and tolerance of antidepressant, safety plan reviewed.

Hematology clinic. 49-year-old male referred for fatigue and exertional dyspnea over two months. Labs: hemoglobin 9.2, MCV 71, ferritin 6, iron saturation 5% — iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy unremarkable, no occult bleeding; dietary iron intake poor. Started on ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with vitamin C, tolerated without GI upset. Plan: repeat CBC and ferritin in 6 weeks, expect hemoglobin rise of 1 g/dL per 2 weeks, continue oral iron for 3 months after normalization, dietary counseling on iron-rich foods.

Pulmonary clinic. 59-year-old female with intermittent wheeze, nighttime cough, and shortness of breath triggered by dust and cold air, relieved by albuterol. Spirometry shows reversible obstruction with 14% bronchodilator response. No sputum production or fevers. Diagnosis: asthma, moderately controlled. Plan: start inhaled budesonide-formoterol twice daily, albuterol as rescue, spacer technique reviewed, asthma action plan provided, avoid triggers, follow up with peak flow diary in 6 weeks.

Neurology clinic: 38-year-old male with 2-year history of Parkinson disease, on carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 TID, today with mild on-off fluctuations; adjusted dosing schedule. Reports excessive worry, restlessness, and recurrent panic attacks with palpitations and fear of dying, GAD-7 score 15, consistent with generalized anxiety disorder with panic attacks; started sertraline, counselled on CBT referral. Also with coldness and claudication in the right calf after walking two blocks, ankle-brachial index 0.7 on the right, consistent with peripheral arterial disease; advised walking program, aspirin, and statin. First metatarsophalangeal joint swelling and tenderness this week, uric acid 9.2, acute gout flare treated with colchicine. Follow-up in 6 weeks.

GI clinic note. 68-year-old male with several weeks of epigastric burning and nausea, worse after meals, no weight loss or bleeding. Exam: mild epigastric tenderness, no masses. EGD showed erythematous gastric mucosa with antral predominant inflammation and mild duodenal erythema; biopsies negative for H. pylori and malignancy. Impression: gastritis and duodenitis, likely NSAID-related — advised discontinuing ibuprofen. Started on pantoprazole 40 mg daily for 8 weeks. Plan: symptom check in 6 weeks, repeat endoscopy only if symptoms persist, dietary modification handout provided.

Telehealth visit: 45-year-old female here for medication refills and chronic issues. Has hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 100 mcg daily; TSH today mildly elevated at 6.8, dose increased to 112 mcg. Her ADHD remains reasonably controlled on lisdexamfetamine; she reports good focus at work, continue current dose. Also complains of persistent bilateral thigh and forearm muscle aches without weakness or trauma — attributed to myofascial soft tissue pain; advised stretching, heat, NSAIDs as needed. Notably, she reports urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia; exam consistent with prostatic enlargement, started on tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly with urology referral. Repeat TSH in 8 weeks.

Pulmonary clinic follow-up. 67-year-old male with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis-predominant type, presents with increased productive cough and dyspnea over the past week but no fever. Longstanding smoking-related COPD; spirometry previously showing fixed airflow obstruction. Exam: scattered expiratory wheezes, prolonged expiratory phase, no peripheral edema. Using tiotropium and albuterol-ipratropium; prescribed a five-day prednisone burst and doxycycline for this exacerbation. Reviewed inhaler technique and action plan; oxygen saturation 93 percent on room air. Plan: vaccination review, pulmonary rehab referral, follow-up in two weeks, and return sooner for worsening symptoms or oxygen desaturation.

Vascular clinic follow-up. 53-year-old male presents with bilateral calf cramping after walking two blocks, relieved by rest, worse over the past six months. Exam: diminished dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally, ankle-brachial index 0.7 on the right and 0.75 on the left, no ulcers. He also reports chronic right knee pain with stair climbing; exam shows crepitus and mild varus deformity, tenderness along the medial joint line, imaging shows medial compartment narrowing. Started on supervised walking program and cilostazol for the claudication. Knee osteoarthritis managed with acetaminophen, quadriceps strengthening exercises, weight-neutral activity; NSAIDs avoided given vascular disease. Follow-up in three months with repeat ABI.

Orthopedics clinic. 83-year-old female with bilateral knee pain, worse on stairs and standing, stiffness less than 30 minutes. Exam: bony enlargement and crepitus both knees, varus deformity, moderate effusion right knee. X-rays show joint space narrowing and osteophytes, consistent with bilateral knee osteoarthritis. Comorbid atrial fibrillation with flutter on apixaban and metoprolol; rate regular today at 76. Plan: acetaminophen, physical therapy, home exercise program, cane instruction; discussed elective knee arthroplasty; continue anticoagulation without interruption.

Clinic visit. 50-year-old male with burning urination and urinary frequency for two days; urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites consistent with a urinary tract infection, started on nitrofurantoin. He has epilepsy with complex partial seizures on carbamazepine, well controlled, and persistent asthma using an albuterol inhaler and fluticasone, currently without wheeze. Smokes a pack daily; counseled extensively on nicotine dependence and started on nicotine patch with referral to cessation program. Plan: repeat urinalysis after antibiotics, seizure follow-up with levels in 3 months, inhaler technique reviewed, smoking cessation check-in by phone in 2 weeks.

Hospital ward progress note. 79-year-old male admitted with chest discomfort; known coronary artery disease with prior stenting, on aspirin, atorvastatin, and metoprolol for chronic ischemic heart disease. This admission complicated by oliguria and rising creatinine to 3.8 mg/dL from baseline 2.1 mg/dL, consistent with acute kidney injury superimposed on stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Cardiology recommends continuing anti-ischemic therapy; nephrology consulted. Holding lisinopril and NSAIDs, providing IV fluids judiciously, monitoring electrolytes and urine output daily. Creatinine trending down to 2.9 mg/dL. EKG shows no acute ST changes; troponins mildly elevated, attributed to demand ischemia from his underlying CAD. Plan: continue current management, repeat renal panel, and arrange outpatient cardiology follow-up on discharge.

ICU admission note. 53-year-old male transferred from the ED with fever 39.2, tachycardia 118, hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation, confusion, and leukocytosis with bandemia; lactate 4.1 — meeting criteria for sepsis of unclear source. He also reports four days of productive cough; chest imaging without infiltrate but exam with wheezes and rhonchi, consistent with acute bronchitis, felt to be the likely infectious trigger. Blood and sputum cultures drawn. Plan: broad-spectrum antibiotics, continued resuscitation, pressors if needed, bronchodilators, close monitoring.

Urgent care. 20-year-old male with facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and congestion for 10 days, worse after initial improvement — consistent with acute sinusitis. Also reports recurrent abdominal pain relieved by defecation, bloating, and alternating stool consistency over the past year, consistent with irritable bowel syndrome; no alarm features, weight loss, or blood in stool. Burning urination and urinary frequency today; urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites, confirming a urinary tract infection. Exam: facial tenderness over maxillary sinuses, soft abdomen, no peritoneal signs. Plan: amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis, nitrofurantoin for the UTI, symptomatic saline rinses; dietary counseling and antispasmodic as needed for IBS; follow up if symptoms persist.

28-year-old male seen in cardiology clinic. Known coronary artery disease status-post stenting two years ago; on aspirin, atorvastatin, and metoprolol, denies chest pain this visit. He also carries a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, currently seropositive with tenderness and swelling of both wrists and several PIP joints, managed with hydroxychloroquine and referral back to rheumatology. Additionally reports chronic low back pain without radiculopathy, worse with prolonged sitting; exam shows lumbar paraspinal tenderness and limited flexion, straight leg raise negative. Plan: continue cardiac medications with lipid panel and follow-up ECG; rheumatology to consider DMARD escalation; physical therapy and NSAIDs as needed for the dorsalgia.

Hospital ward day 3. 78-year-old female admitted with dyspnea and productive cough. Known COPD on tiotropium and albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers; chest X-ray without infiltrate, exacerbation treated with steroids and nebs, now improving. Long-standing essential hypertension, on lisinopril, BP today 138/78. Labs revealed iron deficiency anemia: hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, MCV 72, ferritin 8 ng/mL; colonoscopy scheduled as outpatient. Started on ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily. Will continue home inhalers at discharge, follow-up with primary care for BP monitoring and repeat CBC.

CCU admission: 51-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus since childhood, on an insulin pump, presented with 2 hours of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm with diaphoresis. ECG showed ST-elevation in the anterolateral leads; troponin markedly elevated — acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction; taken emergently to cath, LAD occlusion treated with a drug-eluting stent. Blood glucose on arrival 312; insulin pump continued with close monitoring, A1c 8.4. Post-procedure course uncomplicated. Plan: dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehab referral, and endocrinology follow-up for intensified insulin management.

Internal medicine clinic. 59-year-old female presenting with fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. Labs show hemoglobin 9.2 with low MCV, iron studies pending; diagnosed with unspecified anemia, started on iron supplementation. History of alcohol use disorder, currently in relapse with heavy daily intake; referred back to addiction medicine, counseled on abstinence. Known coronary artery disease on aspirin and atorvastatin, stable angina only with heavy exertion. Bilateral knee osteoarthritis with crepitus on exam; managed with acetaminophen and quadriceps exercises, NSAIDs avoided given anemia.

Orthopedic clinic. 38-year-old female presents with six months of bilateral knee pain, worse with stairs and prolonged standing, mild morning stiffness under 30 minutes, and crepitus on exam. No swelling or warmth. Weight-bearing radiographs show joint space narrowing and osteophyte formation in both medial compartments, consistent with osteoarthritis of the knee. Exam: mild varus alignment, crepitus with flexion, full range of motion, stable ligaments. Plan: acetaminophen and topical NSAIDs first-line, quadriceps strengthening and home exercise program, weight-neutral low-impact activity such as swimming, physical therapy referral, and consideration of corticosteroid injection if symptoms persist. Follow-up in three months.

87M seen at home visit (housecalls program). Complains of episodic severe left temporal headaches with nausea and light sensitivity, lasting hours, typical of migraine in his prior pattern; treated with abortive medication when needed. Liver panel previously notable for mild ALT elevation; ultrasound today reviewed showing diffuse hepatic steatosis with normal liver size — fatty liver disease without cirrhosis or mass. LFTs mildly abnormal but stable. No alcohol use. Exam: abdomen soft, liver edge palpable 1 cm below costal margin, non-tender. Plan: continue migraine abortive therapy, avoid hepatotoxic agents, weight-stable diet, repeat ultrasound and hepatic panel in 6 months, counsel on warning signs of hepatic decompensation.

Primary care clinic. 88-year-old woman seen for follow-up. Labs from last visit show 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 14 ng/mL, consistent with vitamin D deficiency; started on cholecalciferol 2000 units daily, repeat level in three months. She has a long history of well-demarcated scaly erythematous plaques over elbows, knees, and scalp, consistent with plaque psoriasis, currently controlled with topical clobetasol intermittently; skin exam today shows mild scaling at the knees. She also carries a diagnosis of PTSD following the loss of her husband in a motor vehicle accident years ago, with nightmares, hypervigilance, avoidance of driving past the site, and flashbacks; these symptoms have worsened recently around the anniversary. Currently on sertraline with trauma-focused therapy. Plan: continue vitamin D, topical steroids PRN, increase trauma therapy sessions, screen for depression next visit.

Cardiology clinic. 66-year-old female with known coronary artery disease, prior drug-eluting stent to the LAD three years ago, on aspirin, atorvastatin, and metoprolol; today denies chest pain at rest but reports predictable exertional heaviness climbing stairs, consistent with stable angina from chronic ischemic heart disease. ECG shows old anterior changes, no acute findings; stress testing ordered to reassess ischemic burden. She also describes recurrent postprandial right upper quadrant pain, particularly after fatty meals, with ultrasound demonstrating multiple gallstones and a mildly thickened gallbladder wall without ductal dilation, consistent with cholelithiasis. Plan: continue antianginal regimen, consider increased beta-blocker dose, surgical consultation regarding elective cholecystectomy, low-fat diet advice, and return immediately for severe or prolonged pain.

Dermatology clinic. 47-year-old female presents with a pruritic, erythematous eczematous rash over the flexural surfaces of her elbows and ankles, recurring for months, with lichenification on exam; diagnosed with chronic atopic dermatitis, treated with triamcinolone ointment and a fragrance-free emollient regimen. She additionally has rheumatoid arthritis, seropositive, with symmetric synovitis of the MCP and PIP joints and elevated anti-CCP, on methotrexate weekly with folic acid and hydroxychloroquine; disease moderately active with morning stiffness about 45 minutes. No skin infection noted. Plan: continue topical steroids with taper, wet wraps if flaring, methotrexate dose escalation considered, rheumatology follow-up in 8 weeks, return sooner if rash worsens or joints flare.

43-year-old female seen in clinic for cough, low-grade fever, sore throat, and myalgias of 3 days; exam with pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no focal consolidation — consistent with a viral illness; supportive care advised, no antibiotics. Her COPD remains stable on tiotropium and albuterol; spirometry previously showing non-reversible obstruction; advised to monitor for exacerbation. Epilepsy well controlled on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily; no seizures in 14 months; driving restrictions reviewed. She also reports intermittent epigastric burning; exam with mild epigastric tenderness; likely gastritis, started on pantoprazole 40 mg daily, H. pylori testing ordered, counselled to avoid NSAIDs. Follow-up in 6 weeks.

Hospital ward note. 77-year-old male admitted with 3 days of oliguria and rising creatinine; acute kidney injury superimposed on baseline. History of hepatic steatosis on prior imaging with mildly elevated transaminases. Admission labs: creatinine 4.1 mg/dL from baseline 1.2, BUN 62, AST 58, ALT 64, ultrasound showing echogenic liver consistent with fatty infiltration without obstruction. Renal ultrasound: no hydronephrosis. Exam: dry mucous membranes, no jaundice or asterixis. Assessment: acute kidney failure, likely prerenal, plus non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Plan: IV fluids, hold nephrotoxic agents, monitor urine output and daily creatinine, repeat LFTs, nephrology consult.

Hospital ward progress note. 57-year-old male with long-standing type 1 diabetes mellitus admitted for insulin titration and diabetic education after repeated morning hyperglycemia. Onset in his early twenties; has been insulin-dependent since diagnosis. Currently on a basal-bolus regimen with lispro before meals and glargine at bedtime. CGM download shows mean glucose 210 mg/dL with frequent overnight spikes; A1c 9.1%. No ketones on admission, no evidence of hypoglycemia unawareness. Exam unremarkable; feet with intact sensation to monofilament, no ulcers. Plan: increase glargine from 24 to 28 units, adjust carbohydrate ratio to 1:8, nutrition consult, and review sick-day rules. Discharge planned tomorrow with endocrinology follow-up in two weeks and repeat A1c in three months.

55-year-old woman admitted via cath lab after presenting with acute chest pain; ECG showed anterior ST depression and troponins elevated, diagnosing an acute myocardial infarction, treated with PCI and stenting. History of obstructive sleep apnea, poor CPAP adherence on the ward, snoring and witnessed apneas documented; sleep medicine to adjust pressures. She reports epigastric burning and nausea; endoscopy showed erythematous gastric and duodenal mucosa without ulcer, consistent with gastritis and duodenitis; started on pantoprazole. Longstanding seropositive rheumatoid arthritis affecting hands and feet symmetrically, on methotrexate and low-dose prednisone; rheumatology consulted regarding antiplatelet and DMARD interactions. Plan: dual antiplatelet therapy, PPI, CPAP retraining, rheum follow-up.

Hospital ward progress note. 64-year-old female admitted from the ED with sepsis of urinary tract origin — fever 38.9°C, tachycardia 118, hypotension responding to fluids, lactate 4.1, positive blood cultures started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. History of alcohol use disorder with prior withdrawal episodes; CIWA monitoring in place, thiamine given, alcohol counseling deferred until medically stable. Chronic eczema on both hands and flexural forearms with lichenified, fissured patches; continued triamcinolone ointment and emollients. Plan: complete antibiotic course, repeat cultures, taper CIWA protocol, add addiction medicine consult, dermatology follow-up for eczema after discharge.

ED note. 26-year-old man presents with fever 38.9 C, tachycardia 118, hypotension 92/50, and confusion; blood cultures drawn, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Source appears urinary per urinalysis; sepsis suspected, aggressive IV fluids started and broad-spectrum antibiotics given. Concurrent iron deficiency anemia, hemoglobin 9.1 with ferritin 8, attributed to poor intake; IV iron deferred until stable. Known irritable bowel syndrome with recurrent cramping and alternating bowel habit, no alarm symptoms. Dorsalgia: chronic mid-back muscular pain, worse with prolonged sitting, no neurologic deficits; NSAIDs and stretching advised. Exam: febrile, tachycardic, soft abdomen, spine tenderness paravertebral without radiation. Plan: admit to ward for sepsis management, monitor lactate and cultures, iron studies on recovery, continue IBS dietary measures, physical therapy referral for back pain.

Telehealth visit, 38-year-old male with idiopathic Parkinson disease, diagnosed two years ago, currently on carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 three times daily with good symptom control aside from mild resting tremor of the right hand. He reports persistent midline low back pain and stiffness, worse with prolonged sitting, without radicularity or red flags; attributed to dorsalgia and postural muscle rigidity. He was found to have vitamin D deficiency on recent labs (25-OH vitamin D level 14 ng/mL). Plan: initiate vitamin D2 50,000 units weekly for eight weeks then 1000 units daily maintenance, repeat level in three months. Continue levodopa, add physical therapy focusing on core strengthening and back flexibility, gentle stretching, and heat as needed. Encourage outdoor activity and dietary vitamin D. Follow up in three months or sooner if back pain worsens.

Family medicine clinic. 31-year-old male evaluated for longstanding inattention, impulsivity, and disorganization affecting job performance. Completed ASRS-v1.1 with high scores in inattention and hyperactivity domains; collateral history from partner confirms childhood onset. Failed organizational strategies alone. No substance use. Exam unremarkable; vitals stable. Assessment: attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, adult. Plan: trial of atomoxetine 40 mg daily titrating to 80 mg, safety labs at baseline, sleep hygiene counseling, follow-up visit in 6 weeks to assess response and side effects.

Dermatology clinic: 69-year-old male presents with persistent scaly plaques on the scalp, elbows, and extensor forearms, intermittently itchy, present for years and worse this winter. Exam: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery scale and pinpoint bleeding on gentle scraping (Auspitz sign), some nail pitting. No joint pain or swelling reported. Biopsy previously confirmed psoriasis vulgaris. Plan: increase topical clobetasol ointment to twice daily on plaques, add topical calcipotriene to scalp, phototherapy discussed if inadequate response in 8 weeks; follow-up in two months.

Internal medicine clinic. 83-year-old male seen for fatigue and increasing dyspnea on exertion over six weeks. Labs: hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 71, ferritin 8 ng/mL, low serum iron, elevated RDW — findings diagnostic of iron deficiency anemia. Colonoscopy and upper endoscopy scheduled to evaluate for a GI source; no overt bleeding reported. Exam: pale conjunctivae, mild pallor, no melena on rectal exam. Plan: oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily with vitamin C, repeat CBC and iron studies in six weeks, and iron infusion considered if oral therapy not tolerated. Counselled on dietary iron sources.

41-year-old female to ED with 18 hours of right lower quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, one episode of vomiting. Pain began periumbilical then migrated. Afebrile initially, now 100.4 F. Exam: guarding and rebound tenderness at McBurney's point, positive Rovsing sign. WBC 14.2 with left shift. CT abdomen with contrast shows dilated appendix with wall thickening and periappendiceal fat stranding — acute appendicitis, non-perforated. Kept NPO, IV fluids, cefoxitin administered. General surgery consulted; taken for laparoscopic appendectomy. Postoperative course uncomplicated, advancing diet, discharged next day with analgesia.

ED note. 52-year-old male presents with two days of intermittent right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right scapula, nausea, and vomiting after a fatty meal. Afebrile, hemodynamically stable. Exam: moderate RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign; no peritonitis. WBC 11.2, normal LFTs and lipase. RUQ ultrasound demonstrates multiple echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing in the gallbladder consistent with cholelithiasis, gallbladder wall not thickened, no pericholecystic fluid, and a negative sonographic Murphy sign — no evidence of cholecystitis; common duct not dilated. Given findings of symptomatic cholelithiasis without complications, treated with analgesia and antiemetics with symptomatic improvement. Discharged with low-fat diet, general surgery referral for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and return precautions for fever, persistent pain, or jaundice.

Rheumatology clinic: 45-year-old female with ADHD, on lisdexamfetamine, attention stable. History of podagra in first MTP joint; current uric acid 9.2 mg/dL — gout, on allopuratol 300 mg daily with colchicine prophylaxis. Today presents with diffuse muscle aches and bilateral leg pain without joint swelling, CK normal, consistent with myalgia and soft tissue pain. No weakness on neuro exam; tender points without inflammation. Plan: continue urate-lowering therapy, target uric acid below 6, NSAIDs as needed for pain, physical therapy, continue stimulant with BP check, follow-up 8 weeks.

ED admission note. 49-year-old female brought in with fever 39.1, rigors, tachycardia 118, hypotension 88/52, and confusion — meets criteria for sepsis; source appears urinary with positive urinalysis, blood cultures drawn. Lactate 4.2, WBC 18.9. Started on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, admitted to ICU. Assessment: sepsis with hypoperfusion, likely urosepsis pending cultures. Plan: serial lactates, cultures at 48 hours to narrow therapy, vasopressors if MAP <65 despite fluids, close monitoring.

Dermatology clinic visit. 84-year-old male presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the extensor elbows, knees, and scalp, present for years and intermittently treated with topical steroids. No joint pain or nail pitting reported today. Exam confirms classic plaque-type lesions over extensor surfaces and scalp margin; no pustules or erythroderma. Plan: continue clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily to plaques for two weeks, add salicylic acid shampoo for scalp involvement, and discuss phototherapy referral if inadequate response. Follow-up in eight weeks for reassessment of plaque burden and treatment response.

Rheumatology clinic. 82-year-old female with thyrotoxicosis — TSH suppressed, free T4 elevated — presenting with weight loss, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance. Additionally has seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis affecting hands and feet, with symmetric synovitis of MCPs and PIPs; currently on low-dose prednisone and scheduled methotrexate. Exam: fine tremor, mild proptosis, tender swollen MCP joints, nodules on extensor surfaces. Plan: endocrinology referral for definitive hyperthyroidism management; hold methotrexate pending thyroid control; continue NSAIDs for joint pain; check bone density given steroid exposure; follow up in 3 weeks.

24M seen at student health telehealth visit for 4 days of sore throat, rhinorrhea, congestion and dry cough — exam via video, no fever, no exudate; diagnosed acute upper respiratory infection, viral etiology most likely. Supportive care: fluids, rest, pseudoephedrine as needed, no antibiotics indicated. Also has a surprising history for his age: osteoporosis confirmed on DEXA last year (Z-score -2.5 at lumbar spine) in the setting of chronic corticosteroid use for a prior kidney condition, no fractures to date. Continuing calcium 1000 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU daily, on alendronate 70 mg weekly prescribed by endocrinology. No new fracture symptoms; back pain absent. Plan: repeat DEXA in one year, endocrinology follow-up already scheduled, return if URI symptoms worsen or fever develops.

Family medicine telehealth visit. 20-year-old female with fatigue, cold intolerance, mild weight gain, and constipation over several months. TSH elevated at 11.2 with low free T4, consistent with hypothyroidism (not autoimmune by negative antibodies); started on levothyroxine 50 mcg daily. She also reports frequent heartburn and sour regurgitation, worse after meals and when lying down, consistent with gastroesophageal reflux disease; advised dietary modification and started on omeprazole 20 mg daily. Plan: recheck TSH in six weeks, lifestyle counseling, PRN antacid, follow-up visit at eight weeks.

Neurology clinic. 66-year-old man with Parkinson disease diagnosed 4 years ago, on carbidopa/levodopa and rasagiline; reports on-period shortening and mild end-of-dose wearing off, tremor controlled, no dyskinesias. Concurrent gastro-esophageal reflux disease with postprandial heartburn and occasional nocturnal regurgitation; on pantoprazole 40 mg daily with incomplete relief, prompting this visit. Exam: hypophonic speech, reduced arm swing left, cogwheel rigidity, stable gait; no red flags on abdominal exam. Plan: add entacapone to extend levodopa effect; advise taking levodopa 30-60 minutes before meals to reduce protein interference; escalate reflux therapy with nighttime H2 blocker and lifestyle measures; reassess in 3 months.

Telehealth visit. 81-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus reports improved fasting glucose readings but occasional morning values in the 160s. He has been adherent to metformin 1000 mg twice daily; glyburide was discontinued last visit due to hypoglycemic episodes. A1c today 7.4%, down from 8.1%. He also endorses persistent fatigue and diffuse muscle aches over the past two months. Labs drawn this week reveal 25-hydroxy vitamin D level of 14 ng/mL, consistent with deficiency; calcium and phosphorus normal. Plan: continue metformin, add cholecalciferol 50,000 units weekly for 8 weeks then maintenance 1000 units daily, repeat A1c and vitamin D level in 3 months, reinforce dietary counseling, annual retinal and foot exam scheduled.

Hospital admission, geriatric medicine. 69-year-old female with Alzheimer disease, moderate stage, brought in by family for fever, cough, and confusion worsening over two days. Exam: temperature 101.2 F, scattered crackles right lower lobe, oxygen saturation 91 percent. Chest x-ray shows right lower lobe infiltrate; pneumonia, organism not yet identified, cultures pending. She also complains of sore throat; pharynx erythematous without exudate, consistent with acute pharyngitis, rapid strep negative. Chronic eczema on flexor forearms is flared; continuing triamcinolone topical cream and moisturizers. Donepezil continued for her dementia. Plan: empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin, supportive care, neurochecks, reorientation measures, dermatitis management, and repeat imaging. Family updated.

Endocrinology clinic: 27-year-old female evaluated for palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, weight loss of 8 lbs, and scant menses. Exam: pulse 112, mild diffuse thyromegaly without nodularity, fine tremor, no exophthalmos. Labs: suppressed TSH <0.01, elevated free T4; diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis, started on methimazole with beta-blockade for symptoms. Concurrent ultrasound performed for mild right upper quadrant discomfort showed bright hepatic echotexture consistent with hepatic steatosis (fatty liver); LFTs mildly elevated, ALT 68. No alcohol use. Plan: repeat thyroid panel in 6 weeks, counseled on diet and weight-neutral habits for fatty liver, repeat hepatic panel in 3 months, avoid hepatotoxic agents, and follow up sooner if jaundice or abdominal pain worsens.

79-year-old male seen in neurology clinic with wife, who provides much of the history. Exam shows bradykinesia, rigidity of both upper extremities, resting tremor of the right hand, and shuffling gait with reduced arm swing — findings consistent with his longstanding Parkinson disease; on carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 three times daily with good response, though he reports end-of-dose wearing off. Over the past two years there has been progressive memory decline, disorientation in unfamiliar settings, and repetitive questioning; MoCA 16/30, consistent with Alzheimer disease; brain MRI shows diffuse cortical atrophy with medial temporal involvement. No hallucinations reported. Plan: add entacapone for wearing off, donepezil 5 mg nightly with titration, caregiver support referrals, driving cessation discussed, follow-up in six weeks.

Inpatient admission: 34-year-old male presented with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. CT angiogram revealed a segmental pulmonary embolism; ECG shows irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves, confirming atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, rate 118, started on a heparin drip. History of colonic diverticulosis on prior colonoscopy; no active GI bleeding, so anticoagulation with apixaban planned after bridging. Echo pending. Plan: heparin, rate control with diltiazem, transition to apixaban, TTE, hematology consult for hypercoagulable workup, dietary fiber counseling for diverticular disease, follow-up Holter monitoring.

Nephrology clinic. 41-year-old female with chronically reduced kidney function, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2 with stable creatinine over the past year, consistent with chronic kidney disease stage 3b. She reports mild fatigue; urine shows trace proteinuria without hematuria. She is on an ACE inhibitor for kidney protection. Exam: BP 128/78, no edema, no pallor. Plan: continue ACE inhibitor, strict avoidance of NSAIDs, low-salt diet, monitor hemoglobin and calcium-phosphate parameters, repeat renal panel and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio in three months, and vaccinate against influenza and hepatitis B given reduced renal function.

Hospital ward progress note. 80-year-old female admitted with acute upper respiratory infection — cough, rhinorrhea, low-grade fever; negative influenza and COVID testing. She has known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with flutter, rate 110 irregularly irregular on monitor, managed with metoprolol and apixaban, which she continues. Exam: scattered upper airway congestion, lungs with few bibasilar crackles, irregularly irregular rhythm without decompensation. Plan: supportive care for the URI, hydration, acetaminophen; continue rate control and anticoagulation; telemetry observed; expect discharge once symptoms improve.

Walk-in clinic: 28-year-old male with a harsh cough productive of yellow sputum for five days, accompanied by sore throat and mild wheeze; lungs clear to auscultation apart from scattered wheezing, no fever, consistent with acute bronchitis. He also reports two days of crampy lower abdominal and suprapubic pain, non-radiating, with mild nausea; abdominal exam shows soft tenderness without rebound or guarding, no mass. Plan: symptomatic treatment for bronchitis with fluids, guaifenesin, and albuterol PRN; urinalysis obtained and unremarkable; reassurance for the abdominal pain with return precautions for localized pain, fever, or vomiting, follow-up in one week if unresolved.

Stroke unit note. 67-year-old female, acute onset right-sided weakness and expressive speech difficulty, last known well 90 minutes prior. Non-contrast head CT without hemorrhage; CT angiography shows occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery, consistent with acute ischemic cerebral infarction. NIHSS 11. Taken for mechanical thrombectomy with successful recanalization; IV thrombolytics administered per protocol. Post-procedure, mild residual aphasia and right arm weakness. Started on high-intensity statin and antiplatelet therapy. Speech and physical therapy consults placed. Swallow evaluation before diet advancement. Blood pressure permissive targets maintained. Plan: telemetry, repeat imaging in 24 hours, stroke education, rehabilitation planning.

Telehealth visit: 37-year-old male with several days of myalgias, low-grade fever, sore throat, and fatigue; exam via video and history consistent with a nonspecific viral illness — supportive care advised, no antibiotics. Also reviewed chronic issues: vitamin D deficiency (level 18 ng/mL) on cholecalciferol 2000 units daily; PTSD with nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance, stable on sertraline 100 mg and trauma-focused therapy, sleep hygiene reinforced; and benign prostatic hyperplasia with nocturia and weak stream, continuing tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly, IPSS improved from 16 to 9. Plan: fluids and rest for viral syndrome, repeat vitamin D level in 3 months, mental health follow-up in 4 weeks, urology as needed.

Urology clinic. 51-year-old male with one week of facial pressure over the cheeks, purulent nasal discharge, and headache, consistent with acute sinusitis; recommended saline irrigation and intranasal steroid, primary care to reassess if symptoms persist beyond ten days. He presents primarily for urinary symptoms: weak stream, hesitancy, nocturia twice nightly, and incomplete emptying for several months. Post-void residual 90 mL, exam shows an enlarged smooth prostate. AUA symptom score 15. Diagnosis of benign prostatic hyperplasia; started on tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly. PSA ordered, reassurance regarding absence of infection. Follow-up in six weeks with symptom diary.

ED visit. 86-year-old male presents with 3 days of a spreading, painful red patch on the left lower leg with warmth, tenderness, and linear streaking proximally, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis; started on cephalexin with elevation, afebrile with normal labs. He reports recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and nausea consistent with migraine, occurring a few times monthly, treated with sumatriptan as needed. He also has sleep difficulties with loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime somnolence; prior home sleep study consistent with obstructive sleep apnea, using CPAP inconsistently. Plan: oral antibiotics with 48-hour recheck, adherence counseling for CPAP, continue triptan with headache diary, follow-up with primary care.

GI clinic, narrative note. 28-year-old female evaluated for months of recurrent abdominal pain relieved by defecation, associated with altered stool frequency and consistency (alternating loose and hard stools), bloating, and no alarm features — weight stable, no rectal bleeding, no nocturnal symptoms. Normal CBC, CRP, celiac serology, and colonoscopy with biopsies unremarkable. Diagnosis: irritable bowel syndrome. Plan: low-FODMAP diet trial, peppermint oil, soluble fiber, stress management, return in 8 weeks.

Hospital ward admission, 54-year-old woman transferred with acute onset left-sided weakness and slurred speech; head CT shows acute ischemic infarction in the right MCA territory, now being managed with aspirin, atorvastatin, and PT/OT. On hospital day two she developed fever, diffuse watery diarrhea, and left lower quadrant cramping; stool studies positive for infectious gastroenteritis/colitis, treated supportively with IV fluids. She also complains of sore throat with erythema on exam, consistent with acute pharyngitis. Right upper quadrant ultrasound performed for RUQ discomfort demonstrates multiple gallstones without cholecystitis. Plan: continue stroke protocol, ciprofloxacin for colitis, symptomatic throat care, surgical consultation regarding cholelithiasis.

Family medicine clinic. 58-year-old male here for follow-up of several chronic issues. His attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder remains managed with methylphenidate ER 36 mg each morning; he reports improved focus at work. He has had a productive cough for 5 days with scattered rhonchi but no fever or consolidation on exam, consistent with acute bronchitis; treated supportively. Right upper quadrant ultrasound performed last month for intermittent postprandial discomfort showed multiple gallstones without wall thickening or ductal dilation; cholelithiasis noted, surgery discussed but deferred. He also has longstanding rheumatoid arthritis affecting MCP and PIP joints symmetrically, with morning stiffness over an hour, on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and folic acid. Plan: continue current medications, symptomatic cough care, GI referral discussion, rheumatology follow-up.

Internal medicine clinic, SOAP. 82-year-old man with stage 3b chronic kidney disease, baseline creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, eGFR 40; nephrology following, avoiding NSAIDs and contrast. Presents with 3 days of rhinorrhea, sore throat, and dry cough; no fever, lungs clear. Acute upper respiratory infection, viral etiology presumed; supportive care advised. Chronic plaque psoriasis involving elbows and knees, currently controlled on topical clobetasol and vitamin D analogue; patches mildly scaly but not flared. A: acute URI; psoriasis, stable; CKD stage 3b. P: fluids and rest, acetaminophen only for discomfort given renal function; continue topical regimen; repeat BMP in 4 weeks; return if fever or worsening dyspnea.

Dermatology clinic. 72-year-old female evaluated for persistent worry, restlessness, difficulty sleeping, and recurrent panic attacks with palpitations and fear of dying over the past year; she also has chronic eczema with pruritic, dry, scaly patches on flexor surfaces of both arms and posterior neck, flaring intermittently. Exam: anxious affect; lichenified erythematous plaques with excoriations on antecubital fossae bilaterally. Plan: escitalopram 10 mg daily for generalized anxiety with panic features, consider CBT referral; for eczema, triamcinolone 0.1% ointment BID x2 weeks, liberal emollient use, fragrance-free skin care; follow-up in 6 weeks for both anxiety response and dermatitis control.

Telehealth visit. 74-year-old woman with several months of heat intolerance, palpitations, 8-pound weight loss, and tremor. Exam via video: fine hand tremor, tachycardia at 108, mild proptosis. Labs: TSH suppressed at <0.01, free T4 elevated at 3.2 — findings consistent with thyrotoxicosis; started on methimazole with beta-blocker for symptom control. She also reports gnawing upper abdominal pain, nausea after meals, and occasional coffee-ground emesis; prior EGD showed erythema of the gastric antrum and duodenal inflammation consistent with gastritis and duodenitis. Currently on pantoprazole twice daily with partial relief. Plan: repeat thyroid panel in six weeks, CBC with differential before starting methimazole (already drawn), continue PPI, avoid NSAIDs, GI follow-up EGD to assess healing, endocrinology recheck.

Hospital admission. 89-year-old female presented to the ED with sudden dyspnea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. CTA of the chest demonstrates a filling defect in the right main pulmonary artery consistent with pulmonary embolism; started on IV heparin with transition to apixaban planned. Exam: tachypneic, O2 saturation 88% on room air improving to 96% on 2 L nasal cannula; no leg swelling on Doppler ultrasound. Her lipid panel from admission shows LDL 162 and triglycerides 210, reflecting known hyperlipidemia; statin therapy to be resumed once acute illness stabilizes. Plan: anticoagulation, serial monitoring, cardiology input on anticoagulation duration, and discharge planning with home oxygen reassessment.

83-year-old male evaluated in the ED for severe throbbing left-sided headache with photophobia and nausea, characteristic of his recurrent migraines; no fever or neurologic deficit, CT head negative. He is in atrial fibrillation with irregularly irregular rhythm at 92 bpm, rate-controlled; on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, which he has taken as prescribed. Exam otherwise benign except mild photophobia. Plan: IV fluids and metoclopramide for migraine relief with discharge once symptoms improve; continue anticoagulation, arrange follow-up with cardiology for rhythm monitoring, and review headache triggers with his primary physician.

Family clinic, 43F with bilateral knee pain, worse with stairs and prolonged standing, morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Exam: crepitus both knees, mild medial joint line tenderness, no effusion — consistent with bilateral osteoarthritis of the knees. BMI 31.4; weight-reduction plan discussed with dietitian referral, target 7% loss. She also reports ongoing PTSD symptoms after a motor vehicle accident — flashbacks, avoidance, poor sleep; established with counseling, continued sertraline 100 mg daily. Knees: quadriceps strengthening, acetaminophen PRN, consider PT. Follow-up 8 weeks.

59-year-old male in rheumatology clinic for seropositive erosive rheumatoid arthritis. On methotrexate 20 mg weekly and adalimumab every other week; currently he has synovitis of the MCP and wrist joints bilaterally and morning stiffness over an hour. He also reports burning urination and urgency for two days. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria; given his immunosuppression, antibiotics started promptly. Plan: continue current DMARD/biologic regimen with hold on methotrexate dose escalation until infection clears; start ciprofloxacin for the urinary tract infection, repeat urine culture, and reassess synovitis at next visit.

89M brought to geriatrics clinic by daughter with 3 months of weight loss (14 lbs), tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance, and irritability. Exam: AF? no — regular tachycardia 110, fine hand tremor, warm moist skin, mild proptosis, thyroid diffusely enlarged and nontoxic, no bruit. Labs: TSH suppressed < 0.01, free T4 elevated at 3.2, consistent with thyrotoxicosis, most likely toxic multinodular goiter vs Graves; will obtain uptake scan. Given his age and fall risk, started low-dose methimazole 5 mg daily and propranolol 20 mg TID for rate and tremor, holding anticoagulation question pending atrial fibrillation evaluation with Holter. Endocrinology referral, repeat TFTs in 4 weeks, counseled family on red flags including chest pain and confusion.

Hospital admission, 76-year-old female transferred from ED with several days of fatigue, low-grade fever, myalgias, and sore throat consistent with a viral syndrome. She also reports heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, and 8-lb weight loss over two months. Labs: suppressed TSH, elevated free T4, consistent with thyrotoxicosis. Abdominal ultrasound performed for RUQ discomfort reveals multiple gallstones without cholecystitis. Creatinine rose to 2.9 mg/dL from baseline 1.0 with oliguria, felt to be acute kidney failure, likely prerenal/viral-related. Plan: IV fluids, nephrology consult, supportive care for viral illness, endocrinology consult for hyperthyroid management, serial renal labs, low-fat diet given cholelithiasis, surgical consult as needed.

Hospital ward note: 88-year-old female admitted with left lower leg redness, warmth, and swelling spreading proximally over 48 hours, with chills. Exam: temperature 100.8, irregularly irregular pulse at 112, left calf with well-demarcated erythema, edema, tenderness, and a streak of proximal redness along the lymphatic channels; WBC 14.2. Known atrial fibrillation on apixaban, rate adequately controlled; ECG today confirms atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, metoprolol increased. BMI 29.4 with central adiposity on exam; nutrition consult arranged for weight management. Impression: cellulitis with acute lymphangitis of the left lower extremity. Started on IV cefazolin with marked improvement; will step down to oral cephalexin. Continue anticoagulation.

Hospital admission, 75-year-old female. Presented to ED with acute dyspnea and right pleuritic chest pain; CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed a segmental pulmonary embolism, started on IV heparin transitioning to apixaban. She reports longstanding fatigue and cold intolerance; TSH elevated at 11.8 with low free T4, consistent with hypothyroidism — levothyroxine 50 mcg daily initiated. Exam of the left lower leg reveals a warm, erythematous area with tenderness tracking proximally along lymphatic vessels, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis; treated with IV cefazolin. She also reports diffuse lower abdominal and pelvic pain; CT abdomen unremarkable, pain managed supportively while under observation. Plan: continue anticoagulation, antibiotics, thyroid replacement, monitor pain, repeat labs.

Telehealth visit: 29-year-old male established for essential hypertension, home readings averaging 152/96 on lisinopril 20 mg daily; will increase to 40 mg. Reports intermittent left lower quadrant discomfort; prior colonoscopy demonstrated diverticulosis of the colon, flare managed with clear liquid diet and fiber supplementation. Also notes urinary frequency, weak stream, and nocturia x2; IPSS 12, prostate exam shows smoothly enlarged gland consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia; started tamsulosin 0.4 mg nightly. Plan: repeat BP check in 2 weeks, increase dietary fiber, follow up on urinary symptoms, CMP in 3 months.

Telehealth follow-up, 38-year-old man with known coronary artery disease status post drug-eluting stent to the LAD two years ago. Reports stable exertional chest heaviness, occasionally relieved by rest. Also wheezing and nighttime cough, worse with cold air and exercise. Medications: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily; albuterol inhaler PRN with frequent use recently. Plan: continue anti-ischemic regimen, schedule stress perfusion imaging, add low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with long-acting beta agonist for asthma control, review inhaler technique, and follow up in four weeks.

ED visit. 63-year-old male presents with severe sore throat, odynophagia, and fever for two days. Exam: temperature 38.4 C, pharynx markedly erythematous with tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical adenopathy — acute pharyngitis, rapid strep positive; started penicillin VK. He is known hypertensive, blood pressure 178/104 in triage, 168/98 on repeat; home lisinopril ran out two weeks ago — essential hypertension uncontrolled; prescription renewed and adherence counseled. Labs show creatinine 2.2 from baseline 1.1 with oliguria and mild dehydration, acute kidney injury likely prerenal; given IV fluids, creatinine improved to 1.6 before discharge. Discharged with ENT follow-up not needed; primary care follow-up in 3 days for repeat renal panel and blood pressure check. Return if unable to swallow fluids.

Clinic follow-up, 66-year-old female here for fatigue, cold intolerance, and mild constipation over the past several months. She takes levothyroxine 75 mcg daily but admits to missing doses recently. Exam: dry skin, mild periorbital puffiness, pulse 58, no goiter or thyroid nodularity. TSH today 12.4, free T4 low-normal. Impression: hypothyroidism, suboptimally controlled, likely secondary to erratic replacement dosing. Plan: reinforce daily adherence, increase levothyroxine to 88 mcg daily, recheck TSH in 8 weeks. Advised symptoms should improve with consistent therapy.

Clinic visit. 60-year-old male presents with three months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and unusual cravings for ice. Denies melena or hematochezia but reports occasional dark stools. Exam: pale conjunctivae, resting tachycardia 104 bpm, systolic flow murmur at left sternal border. Labs: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL, iron saturation 5%. Consistent with iron deficiency anemia; colonoscopy and upper endoscopy scheduled to evaluate for a GI source. Started on oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily with vitamin C, stool occult blood testing ordered. Will recheck CBC and iron studies in six weeks. Advised on dietary iron sources and follow-up sooner if melena or lightheadedness develops.

Telehealth cardiology follow-up. 80-year-old female with known atrial fibrillation and flutter reports intermittent palpitations but no syncope, chest pain, or dyspnea. She remains on apixaban for stroke prevention and diltiazem for rate control. Home readings show irregular pulse 70-90 bpm; ECG from last week demonstrated the characteristic irregularly irregular rhythm with flutter waves. Exam via video unremarkable; no signs of decompensation. Plan: continue current anticoagulation and rate control, repeat ECG in three months, monitor renal function for apixaban dosing, and return sooner if sustained rapid palpitations, lightheadedness, or bleeding occur.

Telehealth visit. 45-year-old female with history of post-traumatic stress disorder on sertraline 100 mg daily, reports ongoing nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance of crowds after a motor vehicle accident two years ago; trauma-focused CBT continuing. She also has gastro-esophageal reflux disease controlled with omeprazole 20 mg daily, though occasional heartburn at night. Reports left calf swelling and tenderness for three days; sent for duplex ultrasound which showed acute deep vein thrombosis of the left lower extremity. Started on apixaban 5 mg BID. Additionally complains of chronic lower back dorsalgia; recommended NSAID avoidance given anticoagulation, using heat and PT. Follow-up in one week with PCP; PTSD medication adherence reviewed.

Neurology clinic follow-up. 28-year-old male presents with progressively worsening resting tremor of the right hand, bradykinesia, and decreased arm swing on the right over the past year. Exam: masked facies, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, impaired finger tapping, positive pull test. No family history of early-onset parkinsonism; genetic panel declined for now. Started on carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 three times daily with good response; pramipexole held off. Physical therapy and speech referral placed. Will reassess in 3 months with UPDRS scoring. Diagnosis of Parkinson disease discussed with patient and family; deep brain stimulation discussed as future option if medication response wanes.

Pulmonary clinic. 66-year-old male with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presenting with three months of increasing dyspnea and chronic productive cough. Spirometry: FEV1/FVC 0.55, minimal bronchodilator response. Exacerbations twice last year. Currently on tiotropium daily and albuterol PRN; adding flutropium-formoterol combination inhaler, pulmonary rehabilitation referral, and updating his action plan. Also, recent DEXA scan obtained for loss of height shows low bone density of the spine and hips without fracture — osteoporosis. Started on alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation. No fractures on imaging. Follow-up in three months with repeat spirometry; return sooner for worsening breathlessness.

Outpatient internal medicine clinic. 28-year-old male here for follow-up of type 1 diabetes mellitus on insulin glargine and lispro; A1c 7.4%. He describes two months of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and weight loss consistent with a major depressive episode, single episode; started on sertraline 50 mg daily. His ADHD remains active with persistent inattention and disorganization; methylphenidate LA continued. Exam: BMI normal, abdomen benign. Ultrasound shows hepatic steatosis; LFTs mildly elevated; diagnosed with fatty liver disease; advised to limit alcohol and follow low-fat diet. Plan: endocrinology follow-up, repeat LFTs in six weeks, PHQ-9 monitoring.

Hospital admission. 68-year-old woman brought to the ED with 24 hours of right lower abdominal pain, vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. Exam reveals localized right lower quadrant tenderness with rebound and a positive psoas sign; temperature 101.1 F, heart rate 104. CBC shows leukocytosis of 16.8 with neutrophil predominance; CRP elevated. CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrates an enlarged, fluid-filled appendix with wall hyperenhancement and surrounding inflammatory changes consistent with acute appendicitis without abscess or perforation. Patient taken for laparoscopic appendectomy; uncomplicated procedure. Postoperative plan: IV antibiotics, gradual diet advancement, and discharge planning once tolerating oral intake.

55-year-old female hospitalized on telemetry after witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Known epilepsy, on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily; levels subtherapeutic, so dose increased to 750 mg twice daily. She describes poor sleep with witnessed apneas and daytime somnolence; overnight oximetry shows recurrent desaturations consistent with obstructive sleep apnea — sleep medicine consulted, CPAP to be initiated. Chest x-ray reveals a right lower lobe infiltrate; she has fever, crackles at the right base, and elevated WBC, felt to be pneumonia, organism not yet identified. Plan: ceftriaxone and azithromycin, seizure precautions, CPAP titration, and EEG follow-up after discharge.

Telehealth follow-up. 77-year-old male with prior ischemic stroke, residual mild right-hand weakness, continues aspirin and atorvastatin. BMI 29.4; we discussed weight-reduction diet and daily walking. He smokes half a pack daily with nicotine dependence; encouraged cessation, offered nicotine patch and counseling referral. Continues to experience nightmares, hypervigilance, and flashbacks related to prior military trauma; PTSD symptoms stable on sertraline 100 mg, no suicidal ideation. No new neurologic deficits reported. Plan: repeat carotid duplex, dietitian referral, PTSD therapy appointment, follow-up in 3 months.

Primary care clinic. 77-year-old female presents with three days of sore throat, nasal congestion, and dry cough consistent with acute upper respiratory infection; supportive care advised, no antibiotics indicated. She also describes two days of acute pain, swelling, and redness of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint, unable to tolerate a sock; uric acid 8.9 mg/dL, consistent with a gout flare; started on colchicine and counseled on purine-limited diet. Routine labs show 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 14 ng/mL, confirming vitamin D deficiency; prescribed cholecalciferol 2000 units daily with recheck in three months. Follow-up as needed for worsening respiratory symptoms.

ED visit. 23-year-old male with 24 hours of watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and low-grade fever after eating undercooked chicken at a food truck. Stool studies sent; WBC mildly elevated. Hydrated with IV fluids and discharged with antiemetics for infectious gastroenteritis and colitis. During screening he reports smoking half a pack daily for five years; counseled on nicotine dependence, offered nicotine replacement and cessation program. He also describes flashbacks and nightmares since returning from deployment, avoids crowds, hyperarousal consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder; referred to veterans' behavioral health, started sertraline 50 mg daily. Return precautions for dehydration given.

Geriatric clinic. 73-year-old female brought in by daughter for cognitive decline and fatigue. Daughter reports progressive memory loss over two years, getting lost in familiar places, repeating questions — consistent with Alzheimer disease, moderate stage; donepezil 10 mg daily continued. TSH elevated at 12.4 with low free T4, consistent with hypothyroidism other than primary autoimmune etiology after prior thyroid surgery; levothyroxine increased to 100 mcg daily. She also reports dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency for two days; urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites, consistent with urinary tract infection, treated with nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for five days. Repeat TSH in six weeks. Caregiver support and safety measures reviewed.

Inpatient admission. 28-year-old male admitted with one week of palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss of 8 lbs, tremor, and anxiety. Exam: heart rate 118 irregular, mild proptosis, fine hand tremor, warm moist skin, thyroid diffuse and mildly enlarged. TSH suppressed below 0.01, free T4 elevated at 3.8 — thyrotoxicosis, Graves likely; started methimazole 10 mg twice daily and propranolol 40 mg three times daily. Concurrent fever, productive cough with rusty sputum, pleuritic right-sided chest pain; chest X-ray shows right lower lobe infiltrate, pneumonia, unspecified organism; ceftriaxone and azithromycin initiated. Endocrinology consulted. Cardiac monitoring shows sinus tachycardia with occasional ectopy. Improving on therapy; thyroid uptake scan planned after acute illness resolves.

46M clinic follow-up. Chronic kidney disease known, today eGFR 42 with creatinine 1.8, stable from prior values; continue nephrology co-management, avoid NSAIDs. Reports intermittent left lower quadrant cramping relieved with bowel movements; CT colonography from last month demonstrates multiple sigmoid diverticula without inflammation — diverticulosis managed with high-fiber diet. Bilateral knee pain worse with stairs, crepitus on exam, tibiofemoral joint line tenderness; imaging confirms bilateral compartmental osteoarthritis — physiotherapy referral, acetaminophen as needed (NSAIDs avoided given CKD). Vitamin D 25-OH level 14 ng/mL; start ergocalciferol 50,000 IU weekly x8 weeks then maintenance. Return in 3 months with repeat metabolic panel and vitamin D level.

29-year-old female admitted to the ward after ED presentation for evaluation of alcohol use disorder — daily heavy drinking, morning tremor, and prior withdrawal seizure; started on CIWA protocol and thiamine. Labs: hemoglobin 9.2 with MCV 76, ferritin 8, consistent with iron deficiency anemia; stools guaiac negative, diet poor in iron, started on ferrous sulfate. Colonoscopy performed for anemia workup incidentally reveals diverticulosis of the descending colon without evidence of bleeding or diverticulitis; advised high-fiber diet. Exam: pallor of conjunctiva, no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Plan: inpatient alcohol withdrawal management, addiction consult for relapse prevention, iron repletion with repeat CBC in six weeks, dietary counseling, follow-up with GI as needed.

Hospital ward note. 43-year-old female admitted with acute myocardial infarction; presented with crushing substernal chest pain, troponin I peaked at 8.2, ECG showed ST elevation in inferior leads, urgent PCI with stent to the right coronary artery. She also has fever 38.4 C, productive cough, and right lower lobe infiltrate on chest imaging consistent with pneumonia, unspecified organism; started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin. She reports chronic mid-back dorsalgia, managed with heat and acetaminophen. Baseline creatinine 1.8 with eGFR 38, known chronic kidney disease stage 3b; nephrology consulted, renally dosing medications. Cardiology and hospitalist co-managing; aspirin, ticagrelor, and atorvastatin continued.

38-year-old female seen in rheumatology clinic for recurrent right first MTP joint pain, now also in left ankle. Episodes of acute monoarticular swelling with erythema and exquisite tenderness, worse at night, previously responsive to NSAIDs. Serum uric acid 8.9 mg/dL. She also reports chronic mid and lower back pain, aching, non-radiating, exacerbated by prolonged standing; exam shows paravertebral tenderness without neurologic deficits. Started allopurinol 100 mg daily with titration plan, colchicine 0.6 mg for flares. For the dorsalgia: PT referral, heat, NSAIDs as needed, core-strengthening exercises. Follow-up in 6 weeks with repeat uric acid.

ICU admission note: 40-year-old female transferred from ED with fever, hypotension, and confusion; blood cultures drawn, lactate 4.2, meeting criteria for sepsis of unclear source, started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluids. She also presented with crushing substernal chest pain; ECG showed ST elevations in the inferior leads and troponin I markedly elevated, consistent with an acute myocardial infarction; urgent cath performed. Source identified as a spreading left lower leg infection with a tender erythematous streak tracking up the medial calf, clinical cellulitis with acute lymphangitis. Baseline creatinine 2.1, eGFR 38, consistent with her known chronic kidney disease stage 3b; nephrology consulted, contrast minimized. Plan: antibiotics, cardiology and nephrology follow-up, wound monitoring.

Hospital ward admission. 86-year-old female admitted with several days of malaise, low-grade fever, myalgias, and rhinorrhea; rapid influenza panel negative, clinical picture felt to be a viral illness of unclear source; supportive care given. Labs show hemoglobin 8.9 with microcytic indices and low ferritin, consistent with iron deficiency anemia; GI workup pending; IV iron started. She acknowledges daily heavy alcohol use with prior withdrawal episodes; diagnosed with alcohol use disorder; thiamine given, addiction team consulted, disulfiram discussed for after discharge. Plan: continue hydration, iron repletion, abstinence counseling, and repeat CBC prior to discharge.

Hospital ward progress note. 89-year-old male admitted with increased sputum purulence and dyspnea — acute exacerbation of his COPD; on tiotropium, salmeterol/fluticasone, prednisone taper, and oxygen 2 L NC. His longstanding rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetric hand deformities; continues low-dose methotrexate. Urinalysis shows pyuria and positive nitrites with dysuria — urinary tract infection, treated with ciprofloxacin. He also has benign prostatic hyperplasia with hesitancy and weak stream, on tamsulosin; post-void residual 120 mL. Plan: continue nebulizers and steroids, complete antibiotic course, monitor renal function, urology follow-up for BPH, rheumatology co-management.

GI clinic. 47-year-old female with recurrent left lower quadrant cramping, bloating, and altered bowel habit over the past year, with one prior episode of fever and marked LLQ pain requiring antibiotics. CT colonography performed last month showed multiple diverticula in the sigmoid colon without acute complications. Exam: soft abdomen, mild LLQ tenderness without peritoneal signs. Impression: diverticular disease of the colon, currently in quiescent phase. Plan: high-fiber diet, fiber supplement (psyllium) daily, adequate hydration; avoid NSAIDs; return immediately for fever, severe pain, or bleeding; colonoscopy consideration once acute concerns resolve; follow-up PRN and in 6 months.

Cardiology clinic. 69-year-old female with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 35%) on lisinopril, carvedilol, and spironolactone; mild ankle edema, lungs clear, daily weights stable. She describes months of excessive worry, restlessness, muscle tension, and episodes of sudden palpitations and fear of dying lasting 10 minutes — generalized anxiety with panic attacks; started sertrol, referred for CBT. She also reports recurrent abdominal pain with bloating, alternating bowel habit, and relief with defecation — irritable bowel syndrome; dietary modification and peppermint oil advised. Plan: repeat echo in 3 months, labs next visit, psychiatric follow-up for anxiety.

ED visit. 81-year-old female with 3 days of right lower leg redness, swelling, warmth, and pain, now spreading up the calf with a red streak toward the ankle. Fever 38.2 C. Exam: erythema with tenderness over the shin, spreading borders, palpable inguinal nodes, streaking consistent with lymphangitis. WBC 15.2. Cellulitis with acute lymphangitis diagnosed; admitted for IV cefazolin, leg elevation, and marking of margins. Diabetic screen negative. Afebrile at 24 hours; transition to oral cephalexin planned once improving, with outpatient follow-up.

36M telehealth visit. Reports loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime sleepiness (Epworth 16); home sleep study confirms obstructive sleep apnea with moderate severity — sleep disorder treatment initiated with CPAP trial. Also 3 days of sore throat and painful swallowing without cough, consistent with acute pharyngitis; exam via photo shows pharyngeal erythema without exudate, rapid strep negative. Additionally, diffuse myalgias and bilateral leg pain without weakness, attributed to soft tissue strain from new warehouse work. DEXA ordered for low-impact wrist fracture history last year revealed T-score -2.5 at the hip, confirming osteoporosis without current pathological fracture. Plan: CPAP initiation and titration, supportive care for pharyngitis, NSAIDs and stretching for myalgias, start vitamin D and discuss bisphosphonate, follow-up in 4 weeks.

ED to cath lab. 39-year-old male with one hour of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to left arm, diaphoresis, and nausea. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V2-V4 with reciprocal changes; troponin markedly elevated — acute myocardial infarction, anterior STEMI. Exam: diaphoretic, anxious, blood pressure 148/92, pulse 96, lungs clear. Aspirin 325 mg chewed, ticagrelor loaded, heparin started; emergent coronary angiography performed showing proximal LAD occlusion, treated with drug-eluting stent. Admitted to CCU; plan: dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, cardiac rehabilitation referral, echocardiogram to assess ejection fraction.

Ward progress note. 79-year-old female admitted with three days of productive cough and low-grade fever; chest x-ray clear, consistent with acute bronchitis superimposed on her chronic heart failure. She has NYHA class II heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, on furosemide and lisinopril; mild ankle edema unchanged, lungs with scattered rhonchi but no crackles. Skin exam shows well-demarcated scaly erythematous plaques on elbows and scalp consistent with her longstanding psoriasis, managed with topical corticosteroids. Plan: bronchodilators and supportive care for bronchitis, continue diuretics with daily weights, dermatology to review psoriasis regimen at discharge.

Inpatient admission. 84-year-old male brought in with 3 days of watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps after a family picnic; fecal leukocytes and positive stool culture consistent with infectious gastroenteritis/colitis. Also found to have acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.6 (baseline 1.1), BUN 48, from volume depletion; oliguria noted. Complains concurrently of facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge and tenderness over maxillary sinuses, consistent with acute sinusitis. History notable for PTSD with nightmares and hypervigilance, worsening during hospitalization, on sertraline. Plan: IV fluids, monitor electrolytes and renal function, stool precautions; amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis; hold nephrotoxins; continue sertraline and offer psychology consult for stress reaction symptoms; nephrology consulted for AKI.

Cardiology clinic follow-up. 35-year-old male presents with intermittent palpitations and a sensation of 'racing heartbeat' lasting minutes to hours, occasionally with lightheadedness. ECG today shows an irregularly irregular rhythm without discrete P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation; a prior Holter captured episodes of atrial flutter with sawtooth F waves in lead II. Exam: irregularly irregular pulse ~110 bpm, no murmurs, no thyromegaly, no signs of heart failure. TSH and electrolytes normal, echo unremarkable. Plan: start metoprolol for rate control, initiate apixaban for stroke prevention given CHA2DS2-VO score considerations discussed, cardiology follow-up in 4 weeks with repeat ECG. Discussed rhythm monitoring and ablation options if symptoms persist.

Ward progress note: 76-year-old male admitted with cough, congestion, low-grade fever, and rhinorrhea consistent with an acute upper respiratory infection, likely viral; supportive care, no antibiotics indicated. He carries a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease, currently moderate stage, disoriented to time and requiring cues for care; wife at bedside, cognition medications (donepezil) continued. Home medications include aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, and nitroglycerin prn for his chronic ischemic heart disease — coronary artery disease documented on prior angiography with diffuse disease managed medically. No chest pain during admission, ECG unchanged with old Q waves, troponin negative. Plan: fluids, rest, delirium precautions, continue cardiac regimen, discharge home with wife when URI symptoms resolve.

ED note, 68-year-old female presents with three days of cough, rhinorrhea, and sore throat; exam with erythematous pharynx, no exudate, lungs clear — consistent with acute upper respiratory infection, treated supportively. She also reports two days of left calf swelling and tenderness. Exam: left calf 3 cm larger than right, warmth, positive Homans sign. D-dimer elevated; lower extremity duplex ultrasound demonstrates acute left popliteal deep vein thrombosis. Plan: started apixaban, hematology consulted, outpatient anticoagulation follow-up arranged, symptomatic care for URI, return precautions for bleeding or worsening swelling.

18-year-old male seen in pulmonary clinic. Reports loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, and morning headaches; home sleep study consistent with obstructive sleep apnea, AHI 11. Also uses albuterol inhaler for intermittent asthma with exercise-induced symptoms; mild expiratory wheezing today, no rescue use in the past week. CT abdomen obtained for left lower quadrant cramping incidentally demonstrates sigmoid diverticular disease without acute inflammation. Plan: initiate CPAP with mask fitting; add low-dose inhaled corticosteroid; high-fiber diet and hydration for the diverticulosis with return precautions for fever or localized pain; follow-up in six weeks.

Family medicine clinic. 58-year-old male presents with a chronic itchy, scaly rash on both forearms and the flexor surfaces of his elbows, flaring for several weeks despite over-the-counter hydrocortisone. Exam: BMI 29.4, erythematous, lichenified, excoriated eczematous patches with dry fissures on the antecubital fossae and dorsal forearms, consistent with chronic eczema; no weeping or secondary infection. He admits to frequent scratching, especially at night. Plan: triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily for 2 weeks, liberal emollient use, fragrance-free skin care counseling, oral antihistamine at bedtime for pruritus. Also discussed weight management: provided dietary counseling and structured exercise recommendations given overweight status; referred to nutritionist. Dermatology follow-up if not improving, weight recheck in 3 months.

Outpatient clinic, SOAP. S: 20-year-old male with intermittent cough, wheeze, and shortness of breath triggered by exercise and cold air, worse this month, using albuterol more than twice weekly. Also reports chronic heartburn, sour taste in the mouth, and worsening symptoms at night when lying flat, occasionally waking him coughing. Additionally, diffuse muscle aches and bilateral leg pain after starting a landscaping job, without swelling or injury. O: lungs with mild expiratory wheeze, no stridor; abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness; calves supple, no edema; muscles tender to palpation without weakness. A: mild persistent asthma; GERD; myalgia and limb pain from soft tissue strain. P: start inhaled budesonide daily with albuterol rescue, omeprazole 20 mg daily, avoid late meals and elevate head of bed, NSAIDs and stretching for myalgias, follow up in six weeks with spirometry.

Urgent care. 86-year-old female brought in by her daughter with 5 days of productive cough with yellow sputum, low-grade fever to 100.2 F, sore throat, and mild hoarseness. No chest pain or dyspnea at rest. Exam: temperature 100.0 F, lungs with scattered rhonchi, no wheeze, no consolidatory findings, no egophony, O2 sat 96% on room air. Chest x-ray shows no infiltrate or consolidation — acute bronchitis, likely viral. Plan: supportive care with fluids, rest, guaifenesin, acetaminophen as needed for fever; no antibiotics indicated at this time. Return precautions reviewed for worsening dyspnea, high fever, or confusion. Follow-up with PCP if symptoms persist beyond 2-3 weeks.

Telehealth follow-up: 30-year-old female with fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, and weight gain over 6 months. TSH elevated at 14.2, free T4 low — primary hypothyroidism, likely Hashimoto's given positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies; levothyroxine 75 mcg daily started. She also endorses loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing, unrefreshing sleep, and daytime sleepiness (Epworth 14); STOP-BANG elevated; home sleep study ordered to evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea. No other active problems. Plan: recheck TSH in 6 weeks, titrate levothyroxine, sleep study pending, return sooner if symptoms worsen.

Internal medicine clinic. 82-year-old male presents with several weeks of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and pallor. Labs: hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 71, ferritin 8 ng/mL, consistent with iron deficiency anemia; colonoscopy recently unremarkable, started on oral ferrous sulfate. Lipid panel shows LDL 148 mg/dL; hyperlipidemia managed with atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. DEXA scan reports T-score of -3.1 at the lumbar spine, confirming osteoporosis without any fracture; calcium and vitamin D supplemented, alendronate 70 mg weekly initiated with fall-prevention counseling. Plan: repeat CBC and iron studies in 6 weeks, repeat lipid panel in 3 months, follow-up DEXA in two years.

Hospital admission, 54-year-old female brought to ED with acute dyspnea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. CT pulmonary angiogram shows filling defects in right lower lobe segmental arteries consistent with pulmonary embolism. Labs notable for creatinine rising from 1.1 to 3.4 mg/dL with oliguria, consistent with acute kidney failure; nephrology consulted, held nephrotoxic agents, IV fluids titrated. BMI 31.2, documented overweight/obesity; dietary consult arranged and weight-reduction plan discussed. Started on therapeutic enoxaparin bridging to apixaban. Monitoring: daily creatinine, urine output, repeat CBC. DVT ultrasound of bilateral lower extremities ordered. Discharge planned once renal function stabilizes and anticoagulation therapeutic.

GI clinic: 62-year-old female referred for evaluation of recurrent abdominal and pelvic pain, intermittent and diffuse, plus several months of fatigue, pallor, and exertional dyspnea. Labs: hemoglobin 9.2, MCV 71, ferritin 6, consistent with iron deficiency anemia; stool testing and colonoscopy scheduled to exclude a gastrointestinal source. Exam: pale conjunctivae, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs, no masses. Pain diary suggests no clear dietary trigger; pelvic ultrasound ordered to evaluate pelvic pain etiology. Started on oral iron sulfate 325 mg twice daily with vitamin C, tolerated with mild constipation. Plan: repeat CBC in 4 weeks, complete endoscopic workup, gynecology referral pending imaging, and return sooner for worsening pain or melena.

64-year-old female admitted with decompensated heart failure: 2 weeks of worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral leg edema. History includes ischemic stroke last year with residual mild left arm weakness, COPD on tiotropium, and now right lower leg erythema with warmth and tender red streaking up the medial calf consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis. Exam: JVD, bibasilar crackles, S3, pitting edema 3+, leg erythema with lymphangitic streak. BNP elevated, chest X-ray pulmonary vascular congestion. COPD stable, no wheeze, continue inhalers. Diuresed with IV furosemide, cefazolin for cellulitis, continue aspirin and atorvastatin for stroke prevention. Monitoring daily weights, renal function.

Telepsychiatry follow-up. 28-year-old male presents for ADHD management. Reports persistent difficulty sustaining attention at work, frequent task procrastination, losing items, and restlessness since childhood; symptoms worsened since starting a new desk job. Previously on stimulant therapy with good response. No depression or anxiety symptoms. Exam: alert, restless leg movements, mental status grossly normal. Plan: resume extended-release methylphenidate 20 mg qAM, refer for CBT-based coaching, follow up in 8 weeks with attention symptom checklist.

Hospital ward progress note. 76-year-old male admitted with productive cough and low-grade fever; chest x-ray negative for pneumonia, consistent with acute bronchitis. History of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with flutter, rate controlled on metoprolol and anticoagulated with apixaban. Also has stage 3 chronic kidney disease; creatinine stable at 1.9, eGFR 42. Exam: scattered rhonchi, irregularly irregular pulse, no peripheral edema. Plan: bronchodilator, rest, fluids, continue apixaban with renal dose verification, nephrology values on morning labs.

ICU admission. 51-year-old female brought in with acute myocardial infarction of the inferior wall on ECG with troponin 8.2, taken for urgent catheterization.
