She was found to have urosepsis from a urinary source, blood cultures growing E. coli, hypotensive and tachycardic on arrival requiring vasopressors and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Left leg swelling with positive duplex ultrasound showing a deep venous thrombosis of the left femoral vein; therapeutic heparin started given sepsis-related hypercoagulability. Labs also show markedly low 25-OH vitamin D level; supplementation initiated once tolerating oral intake. Plan: continue heparin transitioning to apixaban, dual antiplatelet therapy, serial troponins, antibiotics guided by cultures, vitamin D repletion, prolonged recovery anticipated.

Telehealth follow-up. 51-year-old female seen 10 days after acute hospitalization for left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke. She reports residual right-sided weakness and mild expressive speech difficulty, improving with therapy. Currently on aspirin 81 mg daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, and continuing outpatient physical and speech therapy. MRI of the brain confirmed an acute infarct in the left MCA territory. Exam: 4/5 strength right grip, mild word-finding hesitancy, no facial asymmetry. Plan: continue antiplatelet and statin therapy, follow-up carotid duplex, repeat neurology visit in 4 weeks, and reinforce stroke warning symptoms.

Neurology clinic. 71-year-old male with Parkinson disease, diagnosed 4 years ago, presents with worsening tremor of the right hand at rest, increased bradykinesia, shuffling gait with reduced arm swing, and intermittent freezing episodes. On carbidopa/levodopa 25/100 three times daily and pramipexole; 'on' periods shortened recently. Exam: masked facies, resting tremor right greater than left, cogwheel rigidity bilaterally, postural instability on pull test. He continues to smoke one pack per day, ~40 pack-year history, and is not ready to quit but agreed to consider cessation aids. Plan: increase carbidopa/levodopa frequency to four times daily, add entacapone trial, physical therapy and gait training referral, smoking cessation counseling with offer of varenicline and nicotine replacement at next visit; follow-up in 6 weeks.

Rheumatology clinic. 43-year-old female with 6 months of symmetric morning stiffness lasting over an hour in MCPs, wrists, and PIPs. RF positive, anti-CCP positive, elevated CRP. Also has essential hypertension, on lisinopril 10 mg daily, BP today 138/84. Exam: bilateral wrist and second/third MCP tenderness with mild synovitic thickening, no deformity yet. Hand X-rays: periarticular osteopenia, no erosions. Assessment: seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, early; essential hypertension. Plan: start methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily, baseline CBC and LFTs, hepatitis serologies; add hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily. Continue lisinopril; avoid NSAIDs given BP. Follow up in 6 weeks.

53-year-old male in clinic for recurrent heartburn and regurgitation, worse after meals and when lying flat, improved with over-the-counter antacids, occurring 4-5 times weekly for several months. Occasional nocturnal cough; no dysphagia or weight loss. Exam unremarkable; abdomen soft, nontender. Clinical diagnosis of gastro-esophageal reflux disease. Counseled on lifestyle measures: smaller meals, avoid late eating, elevate head of bed, limit caffeine and alcohol. Started on omeprazole 20 mg daily before breakfast, 8-week trial. Alarm symptoms reviewed; return sooner if dysphagia, bleeding, or weight loss develops.

Urgent care visit. 66-year-old woman presents with 5 days of sore throat, rhinorrhea, myalgias, and low-grade fever, now with a productive cough. She reports generalized viral-type symptoms since last week. Rapid flu and strep testing negative; respiratory viral panel pending. Exam: T 100.2 F, pharynx mildly erythematous without exudate, scattered rhonchi and occasional wheeze, no consolidation. Chest x-ray unremarkable. Impression: acute viral illness with superimposed acute bronchitis. Plan: supportive care with fluids, acetaminophen as needed, guaifenesin, and albuterol inhaler PRN for bronchospasm. Return if fever persists beyond 72 hours or if dyspnea worsens.

Telehealth visit: 31-year-old male, asymptomatic, following up on labs obtained at an employer wellness screen. ALT 68, AST 52, normal bilirubin and INR. Hepatitis B and C serologies negative; autoimmune panel negative; ultrasound report from outside facility describes increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis, no focal lesions. Fatty liver disease felt most likely; he drinks alcohol rarely. Exam unremarkable; BMI borderline but no other conditions identified. Plan: repeat hepatic panel in 3 months, continue dietary counseling and gradual weight loss, consider fibrosis scoring at next visit, abstain from hepatotoxic medications.

Telehealth follow-up. 69-year-old female with known atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, on apixaban and metoprolol; reports occasional palpitations, no syncope or chest pain. Rate 88 irregularly irregular on patch monitor review. She also reports flaring eczematous dermatitis on both hands — dry, pruritic, fissured patches — worse with frequent handwashing; advised fragrance-free emollients and topical triamcinolone. Plan: continue anticoagulation, TSH checked, dermatitis follow-up photo review in 2 weeks, cardiology visit as scheduled.

ED note. 19-year-old male with left calf swelling, warmth, and pain for three days, worse with walking. Duplex ultrasound shows a non-compressible left popliteal vein consistent with deep vein thrombosis; no pulmonary embolism symptoms, chest clear. He also has longstanding attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, managed with lisdexamfetamine, and reports weak urinary stream and nocturia; exam and prior workup consistent with an enlarged prostate, benign in nature. Plan: admit for initiation of anticoagulation with apixaban, analgesia, leg elevation; urology follow-up for his prostatic enlargement; continue ADHD medication as an outpatient.

ICU admission note. 81-year-old female transferred from the ward with hypotension, fever 102.1 F, tachycardia, and confusion; blood cultures grew gram-positive rods, and she is being treated for sepsis with broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, and vasopressor support. History of asthma, using inhaled budesonide-formoterol, currently without wheeze. She has chronic gastritis and duodenitis on prior endoscopy, managed with pantoprazole, which is continued; no melena. Records also document benign prostatic hyperplasia with urinary hesitancy and nocturia, on tamsulosin, continued during admission. Exam: warm extremities, bounding pulses, soft abdomen, no rebound. Plan: serial lactates, culture-guided antibiotic narrowing, stress ulcer prophylaxis, bladder scan for retention given her BPH, and asthma medication reconciliation.

35-year-old female seen in cardiology clinic. Presents with two months of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral leg swelling. Exam: JVP elevated, S3 gallop, bibasilar crackles, 2+ pitting edema. Echo: reduced ejection fraction with dilated left ventricle, consistent with heart failure; started on lisinopril, carvedilol, and furosemide. Labs notable for 25-hydroxy vitamin D level of 12 ng/mL, consistent with vitamin D deficiency; she reports limited sun exposure and low dairy intake. No chest pain at rest. Plan: cholecalciferol 2000 units daily with repeat level in three months, sodium restriction, daily weights, cardiac MRI scheduled to evaluate etiology, follow-up in two weeks with basic metabolic panel.

34-year-old male with 4-year history of Parkinson disease, on carbidopa-levodopa, presents to ED with 24 hours of periumbilical pain localizing to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, and vomiting. Exam: rigidity from baseline Parkinson's noted, but focal rebound tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point. Afebrile 99.2 F, WBC 13.8. CT confirms acute appendicitis without perforation. NPO, IV fluids, preoperative antibiotics. Neurology consulted perioperatively to coordinate timing of dopaminergic doses around surgery. Underwent laparoscopic appendectomy without complication. Postop tremor slightly increased, medications resumed; PT consulted. Discharged in stable condition.

Internal medicine clinic, 54-year-old female for follow-up. BMI 33.2 kg/m2, consistent with obesity; nutrition referral and structured weight-loss program discussed. She reports drinking six to eight beers daily for the past several years with prior unsuccessful quit attempts; meets criteria for alcohol use disorder; agrees to start naltrexone, enrolled in counseling, advised abstinence. Blood pressure today 152/94, consistently elevated at prior visits; diagnosed with essential hypertension, started on lisinopril 10 mg daily with home monitoring. She also reports intermittent right calf discomfort with walking, relieved by rest; ankle-brachial index 0.78 on the right, consistent with peripheral artery disease; started on daily aspirin, statin discussed, smoking not a factor. Repeat labs and follow-up in four weeks.

88-year-old female seen in the ED from home. Three days of progressive redness, swelling, and warmth of the left lower leg with a spreading red streak up the medial calf, fever 38.6 C, and chills. Exam: erythema with sharply demarcated borders over the left shin, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, streaking consistent with lymphangitis; no ulcer or abscess appreciated, pulses intact. WBC 15.8 with left shift; blood cultures drawn. Findings consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis. Plan: admit to the hospital ward for IV cefazolin, limb elevation, mark erythema border for progression monitoring, transition to oral cephalexin when afebrile with improving margins, dermatology consult if no response in 48 hours, wound care teaching prior to discharge.

ICU admission note. 37-year-old female admitted from ED with fever 38.9, tachycardia 118, hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation and vasopressors, leukocytosis and lactic acidosis — sepsis of non-specified source; blood and urine cultures sent, broad-spectrum antibiotics started. History of chronic kidney disease, baseline creatinine around 2.1; now 2.4, nephrology following, avoiding nephrotoxic agents. Also has long-standing eczema with xerosis, lichenified erythematous patches in flexural areas, currently flaring; dermatitis managed with emollients and triamcinolone ointment during admission. Exam: warm flushed skin, flexural dermatitis, no cellulitis. Plan: continue sepsis bundle, adjust antibiotic dosing to renal function, strict fluid balance monitoring, dermatology consult for eczema management, daily renal panel.

ED presentation. 30-year-old male with 2 days of diffuse abdominal and pelvic pain, crampy in nature, intermittent, associated with nausea but no vomiting. Pain radiates to the suprapubic and lower pelvic region. No fever, no diarrhea. Exam: abdomen soft with diffuse tenderness over lower abdomen and pelvis, no rebound or guarding. No testicular tenderness or hernia. Urinalysis unremarkable, hCG n/a. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast showed no acute pathology. Symptomatic treatment given, pain improved, discharged with instructions to return if worsening.

Hospital admission, 80-year-old female brought in with acute chest pain; ECG shows anterior ST elevation, troponin markedly elevated — acute myocardial infarction; managed with urgent PCI and stenting. She smokes one pack per day for 55 years, acknowledges nicotine dependence, and agrees to try nicotine replacement and cessation counseling after discharge. During admission she developed dysuria and cloudy urine; urinalysis positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase, culture growing E. coli — urinary tract infection, treated with ceftriaxone. She also endorses several weeks of low mood, anhedonia, poor appetite, and hopelessness consistent with a major depressive episode; psychiatry consulted, started sertraline. Plan: cardiac monitoring, smoking cessation support, antidepressant titration, antibiotics.

18-year-old female seen in neurology clinic for follow-up of young-onset Parkinson disease. Reports resting tremor of the right hand and bradykinesia; carbidopa/levitodopa 25/100 three times daily continues to provide benefit, though 'off' periods are lengthening. Exam shows masked facies, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, and slow finger tapping. She also reports dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort for three days without fever. Urinalysis shows positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Plan: continue current antiparkinsonian regimen, add entacapone at next visit if off periods persist; start nitrofurantoin for the urinary tract infection, increase fluid intake, and recheck urine after completion of antibiotics.

GI clinic visit. 58-year-old female with heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, and 8-pound weight loss; TSH suppressed at 0.02 with elevated free T4, confirming thyrotoxicosis. Started on methimazole; endocrinology co-management. She also reports recurrent left lower quadrant cramping relieved by defecation, alternating bowel habit, and bloating without alarm features, consistent with irritable bowel syndrome; prior colonoscopy showed sigmoid diverticula without inflammation, so diverticulosis is also documented. Plan: methimazole with repeat thyroid panel in six weeks, beta-blocker for symptom control, high-fiber diet, antispasmodic as needed for IBS, and counseling on seeking care for fever or localized abdominal pain that could indicate diverticulitis. Follow-up scheduled.

ED visit. 25-year-old female with Raynaud-type peripheral vascular disease reports 3 days of spreading redness and tenderness on the left lower leg with a red streak tracking up the medial calf, fevers to 101.2F. Also carries asthma (albuterol PRN, well controlled) and gout, last flare 4 months ago. Exam: left leg warm, erythematous plaque with lymphangitic streaking, tender first MTP joint bilaterally; pulses intact, distal fingertips show acrocyanosis. Labs: uric acid 8.9 mg/dL, WBC 14.2. Plan: IV antibiotics for cellulitis with acute lymphangitis, transition to oral cephalexin; continue albuterol inhaler; colchicine for gout flare; vascular studies for suspected vasospastic peripheral vascular disorder; recheck in 48 hours.

Outpatient behavioral health clinic. 36-year-old male presents for ADHD follow-up. Reports persistent difficulty sustaining attention at work, frequent task procrastination, losing items, restlessness, and impulsivity since childhood; symptoms confirmed by adult ADHD rating scale (ASRS score high). Exam: alert, restless demeanor, no focal deficits. Continue methylphenidate ER 36 mg qAM, increased from 27 mg due to partial response. CBT referral reinforced. Plan: recheck in 6 weeks, monitor appetite, sleep, and blood pressure; no other conditions identified.

Hospital admission. 85-year-old female admitted from the ED with two days of watery diarrhea, fever to 38.4 C, and diffuse abdominal cramping. Stool studies positive for Campylobacter; consistent with infectious gastroenteritis and colitis. Mild dehydration corrected with IV fluids; no blood in stool, C. difficile negative. WBC 13.2, creatinine at baseline. Tolerating oral intake by hospital day 2; azithromycin started given age and severity. Discharged on day 3 with instructions on oral rehydration, hand hygiene, and dietary advancement. Worsening symptoms or bloody diarrhea should prompt return. Follow-up with primary care in one week.

Walk-in clinic. 51-year-old male with two days of sore throat, odynophagia, and malaise, no cough. Exam: pharyngeal erythema with tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, negative rapid strep and culture. Consistent with acute pharyngitis, likely viral; supportive care advised with saltwater gargles and acetaminophen. He also has a history of asthma, using albuterol rarely; notes some chest tightness and wheeze today, peak flow 78% of personal best. Given viral trigger, advised to increase albuterol to two puffs QID, started a short prednisone taper, and reinforced inhaler technique and action plan. Return if fever persists, breathing worsens, or peak flow drops below 70%.

24F telehealth visit for follow-up of liver enzymes and smoking. Reports smoking half pack daily x6 years, first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking, prior quit attempts failed. Discussed nicotine dependence; started varenicline taper and nicotine lozenges, referred to quitline. Liver panel from last month: ALT 68, AST 52, GGT elevated, viral serologies negative, autoimmune workup negative. Ultrasound shows increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis (fatty liver). Alcohol intake minimal. Advised dietary changes and gradual weight-reduction exercise plan; repeat LFTs in 3 months. No abdominal pain or jaundice. Patient motivated to quit smoking; will recheck in 8 weeks by video visit.

Primary care clinic. 39-year-old female with BMI 31.4, class I obesity; discussed structured nutrition plan and increased activity, referral to weight management program. History of post-traumatic stress disorder following a motor vehicle accident two years ago — nightmares, avoidance of driving on highways, hypervigilance; continuing sertraline and trauma-focused CBT. Also reports episodic migraines, unilateral throbbing pain with photophobia, roughly three per month; kept a headache diary, started on sumatriptan as needed with good response. No red-flag headache features. Plan: recheck weight in 3 months, PTSD symptoms reviewed next visit, abortive therapy refill.

Telehealth follow-up, 66-year-old male. History of alcohol use disorder, currently attempting abstinence with ongoing cravings; attending counseling and taking naltrexone. Reports lifelong difficulty with sustained attention, distractibility, and impulsivity that persisted into adulthood; screened positive for adult ADHD, started on methylphenidate with monitoring. Liver panel shows mild ALT elevation; ultrasound demonstrates hepatic steatosis consistent with fatty liver disease, without cirrhotic changes. Counseled extensively on abstinence from alcohol, which should also improve the steatosis. Plan: repeat hepatic function panel in 6 weeks, alcohol counseling continuation, ADHD follow-up in 4 weeks to titrate stimulant dose, and abstinence verification.

Vascular clinic, 70-year-old female evaluated for bilateral leg aching and heaviness. Exam: tortuous, dilated varicose veins in both lower extremities with mild ankle edema and hyperpigmentation over the medial ankles; duplex shows chronic superficial venous insufficiency with incompetent great saphenous veins — peripheral venous disease. Plan: compression stockings 30-40 mmHg, leg elevation, consideration of venous ablation at next visit. She incidentally reports occasional postprandial right upper quadrant discomfort after fatty meals; abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple cholesterol gallstones without wall thickening or ductal dilation — cholelithiasis. Plan: low-fat diet, surgical consultation offered, return sooner if fever, persistent pain, or jaundice.

Pulmonary clinic: 65-year-old female with worsening cough, congestion, low-grade fever, and myalgias for four days — clinically a viral upper respiratory infection; supportive care advised. She has a 35-pack-year smoking history with ongoing nicotine dependence; motivated to quit, started nicotine patch and varenicline. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with chronic dyspnea and prior spirometry showing fixed obstruction; on tiotropium and albuterol. No purulent sputum, no infiltrate on exam; no antibiotics. Plan: inhaler technique review, repeat spirometry, smoking cessation follow-up in 4 weeks.

Geriatric primary care. 80-year-old male with urinary frequency, dysuria, and cloudy urine; urinalysis positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase; culture sent, started on nitrofurantoin for urinary tract infection. Also evaluated for lifelong inattention, impulsivity, and disorganization newly recognized as attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder per collateral history and screening scales; low-dose methylphenidate initiated cautiously with cardiac monitoring. Plan: recheck culture results, hydration, follow up in 2 weeks to assess urinary symptoms and stimulant tolerance.

21-year-old female presents to outpatient behavioral health with months of excessive worry about work and relationships that she cannot control, difficulty concentrating, muscle tension, and poor sleep. She also describes recurrent abrupt episodes of racing heart, sweating, shortness of breath, and fear of dying that peak within minutes and have led her to avoid driving on the freeway. She denies depression or substance use. Exam unremarkable except mild restlessness. Assessment: generalized anxiety disorder with panic attacks. Plan: start sertraline 25 mg daily titrating upward, refer for CBT, sleep hygiene counseling, follow-up in three weeks.

65M seen in ENT clinic for 7 days of facial pressure, purulent rhinorrhea and fever — exam shows maxillary sinus tenderness and purulent drainage; acute bacterial sinusitis, started amoxicillin-clavulanate x 10 days and saline irrigation. Background: chronic alcohol dependence, ~12 beers daily, drinks despite prior pancreatitis; continued AUD counseling encouraged. Coronary artery disease with prior stents to LAD and circumflex; continuing aspirin, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol; denies chest pain, stable. Also known cholelithiasis — RUQ ultrasound last year showed multiple gallstones; currently asymptomatic, no biliary colic; surgical consultation previously offered, patient deferring cholecystectomy. Plan: finish antibiotics, repeat visit if sinus symptoms persist beyond 10 days, GI/surgery follow-up for gallstones, reinforce alcohol cessation.

ED to inpatient admission: 87-year-old male with known chronic ischemic heart disease (CAD, prior stenting, on aspirin and atorvastatin) and severe COPD on tiotropium and albuterol, presenting with four days of facial pressure, purulent nasal discharge, and worsening dyspnea. Exam: fever 38.2, tenderness over maxillary sinuses, wheezing with prolonged expiration, hypoxia to 88%. Labs notable for creatinine 3.0 from baseline 1.3, consistent with acute kidney injury superimposed on baseline renal function; held nephrotoxins and diuretics. CT sinuses confirms acute sinusitis. Plan: intravenous antibiotics for sinusitis, bronchodilator treatments and steroids for COPD exacerbation, cardiac monitoring given CAD, renal dosing of all medications, and strict fluid balance tracking.

ED visit. 24-year-old male presents with 3 days of sore throat, painful swallowing, and fever; oropharynx erythematous with tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes — acute pharyngitis, negative rapid strep, treated supportively. Also noted to have irregularly irregular pulse at 112, ECG shows absent P waves with fibrillatory waves — atrial fibrillation, new onset; started on rate control with metoprolol and arranged cardiology follow-up for monitoring given young age. Lipid panel from last week flagged total cholesterol 268 and LDL 190 — hyperlipidemia; statin therapy discussed. He endorses depressed mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, and weight loss for two months — single episode of major depression; started sertraline and referred for counseling. Discharged home with close follow-up.

ED admission. 89-year-old male brought from home with fever to 38.9 C, confusion, tachypnea, and hypotension (BP 82/48). Urinalysis shows pyuria and nitrites; lactate 4.2, WBC 18,000. Septic shock picture from urinary source; blood cultures drawn, broad-spectrum antibiotics started, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and vasopressors initiated. Admitted to ICU. No focal neurologic deficits; chest X-ray clear. Plan: cultures, antibiotic de-escalation when speciation returns, hourly urine output monitoring, repeat lactate.

81-year-old male brought to ED with 2 hours of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm, diaphoresis, and nausea. EMS ECG showed ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF. Troponin I 12.4 ng/mL. Diagnosis: acute inferior myocardial infarction. Immediate transfer for primary PCI; culprit lesion in the right coronary artery treated with a drug-eluting stent. Post-procedure: aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, atorvastatin 80 mg. Exam post-PCI: comfortable, lungs clear, no murmur, no jugular distension. Monitoring in CCU with continuous telemetry, serial enzymes, and echo to assess wall motion. Cardiology to follow; family updated.

Cardiology clinic. 52-year-old male with known coronary artery disease — prior drug-eluting stent to the LAD — presents for routine follow-up of chronic ischemic heart disease. Denies chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations. Complains of bilateral knee pain, worse on the right with activity and stiffness after sitting, typical of osteoarthritis. Meds: aspirin 81 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Exam: regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, right knee crepitus and mild effusion, varus alignment. ECG: sinus rhythm, Q waves in anterior leads, no acute changes. Plan: continue antianginal and statin therapy, stress test if symptoms recur, right knee x-ray, acetaminophen for pain given aspirin use, orthopedics referral if conservative measures fail.

37-year-old male at primary care clinic for hypertension follow-up. Home BP readings averaging 152/96 despite lifestyle measures. No secondary cause symptoms; basic metabolic panel normal. Funduscopic shows mild arteriolar narrowing; cardiac exam regular rhythm, no murmurs. Started on lisinopril 10 mg daily. Routine labs revealed elevated ALT 68 and AST 55; right upper quadrant ultrasound showed diffuse hepatic steatosis with normal liver size, consistent with fatty liver; viral hepatitis serologies negative. Alcohol intake minimal. Plan: continue lisinopril with BP recheck in 4 weeks, weight and dietary counseling, repeat LFTs in 3 months, avoid hepatotoxic medications.

Rehabilitation ward progress note. 70-year-old woman admitted 5 days ago with acute ischemic stroke of the left middle cerebral artery territory, presenting with right hemiparesis and expressive speech difficulty; MRI confirmed cerebral infarction. Started on aspirin, atorvastatin, and intensive physical and speech therapy; strength improving in right grip, ambulating 30 feet with rolling walker. Chronic psoriasis vulgaris involving scalp and extensor surfaces, currently quiescent on topical corticosteroid as needed; no new plaques during admission. Exam: right facial droop mild, 4/5 right arm and leg strength, scalp scaling without erythema. Plan: continue stroke recovery therapies and secondary prevention medications, maintain topical psoriasis regimen, discharge planning to skilled nursing facility anticipated in one week.

Telehealth follow-up. 31-year-old male with epilepsy and recurrent tonic-clonic seizures, averaging one to two per month despite levetiracetam 1000 mg BID; reports a nocturnal seizure last week with tongue biting and postictal confusion. He also carries a diagnosis of adult-onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis involving his wrists and knees, on sulfasalazine and low-dose prednisone, with morning stiffness lasting over an hour. No new injuries. Neurologically intact on video review. Plan: increase levetiracetam to 1500 mg BID, check drug level and CBC, seizure diary, driving restrictions reiterated; continue DMARD therapy, order hand X-rays, follow up in 6 weeks or sooner for increased seizure frequency.

65-year-old female seen in vascular clinic for left leg swelling and tenderness of three days' duration. Exam: left calf circumference 3 cm greater than right, warmth, and positive Homan's sign; no ulceration. Duplex ultrasound demonstrates a non-compressible left popliteal vein consistent with acute deep venous thrombosis. She is initiated on apixaban 5 mg twice daily with hematology follow-up and repeat duplex in three months. Also reviewed her DEXA scan from last month showing T-score of -2.8 at the lumbar spine and -2.6 at the femoral neck, consistent with osteoporosis without any fracture. No height loss or vertebral compression on imaging. She continues alendronate 70 mg weekly plus calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Advised weight-bearing exercise and fall precautions. Return to clinic in four weeks or sooner for increased leg pain, chest pain, or dyspnea.

Urgent care, 36F with sore throat x3 days, odynophagia, no cough. Exam: pharynx erythematous with exudate on tonsils, tender anterior cervical nodes — acute pharyngitis, rapid strep negative, treated supportively. Also reports diffuse muscle aches and bilateral calf/limb pain without joint swelling or trauma, consistent with soft tissue myalgia; NSAIDs and rest advised. History notable for PTSD with nightmares and hypervigilance, managed with sertraline and trauma-focused therapy, unchanged. Her mother was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer disease; patient reports increasing forgetfulness; cognitive screening scheduled in clinic. Plan: fluids, acetaminophen, return if fever persists.

Outpatient internal medicine, 75M for chronic bilateral knee pain. Exam shows bony enlargement and crepitus at both knees with varus alignment, reduced flexion, medial tenderness — degenerative osteoarthritis of the knees; scheduled for corticosteroid injection left knee and PT. Abdominal ultrasound done last month for mild transaminitis showed increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis; viral serologies negative, ferritin normal — nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. Advised dietary changes, aerobic activity; repeat LFTs in 3 months. Continue acetaminophen for knees, avoid NSAIDs given liver status.

56-year-old male admitted to the medical ward with two days of watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and low-grade fever after a family cookout; stool studies consistent with infectious gastroenteritis/colitis. He is accompanied by his wife, who notes progressive memory decline over the past two years, repetitive questions, and getting lost in familiar places — consistent with his diagnosed Alzheimer disease, currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. Labs also show 25-OH vitamin D level of 14 ng/mL. Plan: supportive care with IV fluids and electrolyte monitoring for the gastroenteritis; start cholecalciferol 2000 units daily for vitamin D deficiency with level recheck in three months; continue donepezil and arrange cognitive follow-up after discharge.

SOAP note, family medicine clinic. 52-year-old female with one week of cough, initially dry now productive of clear sputum, mild chest congestion, and no fever. Exam: lungs with scattered rhonchi, no wheeze, no crackles, O2 sat 97%, no signs of consolidation. Chest not tender. Assessment: acute bronchitis, likely viral. No antibiotic indicated; advised rest, fluids, and dextromethorphan at night. Given return precautions for fever, worsening dyspnea, or symptoms beyond three weeks. Follow-up as needed. Influenza and COVID testing declined by patient, symptoms low-risk.

Inpatient geriatric medicine note. 51-year-old female admitted from home with fever, rigors, tachypnea, hypotension, and altered mental status; blood cultures positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae and lactate 4.6, meeting criteria for sepsis; source appears urinary, treated with meropenem and aggressive fluid resuscitation. Her family reports three years of progressive memory decline, repetitive questions, disorientation, and impaired instrumental activities of daily living; prior cognitive testing and imaging supported a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease, currently on donepezil 10 mg daily. Plan: continue antibiotics with culture-guided de-escalation, monitor mentation closely as delirium superimposed on dementia, resume donepezil, involve family in discharge planning and home safety assessment.

ED note. 36-year-old female brought in by ambulance with fever 103.1 F, heart rate 122, blood pressure 86/48, respirations 26, and confusion. Labs show lactate 5.2 mmol/L, WBC 18,400, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL. Blood cultures drawn; urinalysis and chest radiograph unremarkable, no clear source identified; sepsis with unspecified organism presumed. She received 30 mL/kg crystalloid, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics started within the hour, and was admitted to the ICU with continuous vital-sign monitoring. Plan: repeat lactate, reassess cultures at 24 hours, vasopressors on standby if hypotension persists despite fluids.

Geriatric ward admission. 87-year-old female from assisted living facility with two days of watery diarrhea, fecal leukocytes positive, stool culture pending, presumed infectious gastroenteritis/colitis after a facility outbreak. Concurrently febrile to 38.6 C with productive cough, left lower lobe infiltrate on chest x-ray, pneumonia of unspecified organism; blood cultures drawn. Exam: diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs, crackles at left base, tachypnea. Treated with IV fluids, empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin, contact precautions. Stool specimens sent for Clostridioides difficile and culture. Advance care directives reviewed with family. Improving diarrhea frequency; continue monitoring intake/output and repeat imaging.

Hospital ward note. 42-year-old woman admitted with 4 days of fever, productive cough with rust-colored sputum, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and dyspnea. Chest radiograph shows dense right lower lobe consolidation; WBC 15,800. Community-acquired pneumonia, organism not yet identified; started ceftriaxone and azithromycin, on supplemental oxygen 2 L with saturation 93%. Also chronic eczema affecting flexures of both arms and hands with xerosis, excoriation, and lichenification; flare attributed to illness and frequent hand hygiene. Exam: crackles and egophony right base; erythematous scaly flexural patches. Plan: continue antibiotics, repeat chest film prior to discharge, escalate topical emollients and resuming triamcinolone ointment for dermatitis, incentive spirometry, follow-up in clinic in one week.

Telehealth consult, 39F referred after a low-trauma distal radius fracture last year. DXA scan: lumbar spine T-score -2.7, left femoral neck -2.5, confirming low bone mass without any current fracture. No acute bony pain today. Started calcium 1000 mg daily and vitamin D 1000 IU daily; discussed alendronate 70 mg weekly, which she will begin. Weight-bearing exercise and fall prevention reviewed. Repeat DXA in two years. Return sooner for any new fracture concern.

Clinic visit. 37-year-old man with a history of claudication and cold intolerance in the left leg, previously found to have an unrelated peripheral vascular disorder, now managed conservatively. Presents today with 3 days of sore throat, odynophagia, and fever; exam shows pharyngeal erythema and tonsillar exudate without membranous tonsillitis, consistent with acute pharyngitis, likely viral; rapid strep negative. Also reports worsening urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia over the past year; exam confirms a smoothly enlarged prostate, benign feeling, consistent with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Plan: symptomatic gargles and hydration for the pharyngitis; continue walking program for the vascular disease with ABI follow-up; start tamsulosin nightly, check PSA, and reassess urinary symptoms in 6 weeks.

ED to surgical service, 82-year-old woman brought in with 24 hours of periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, and low-grade fever. Exam: RLQ guarding with rebound; WBC 15,400; CT confirms acute appendicitis, taken urgently for laparoscopic appendectomy. History includes hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 75 mcg daily (TSH 6.8 on admission, dose adjusted) and long-standing alcohol use disorder with daily vodka intake, reporting morning tremor and prior withdrawal seizures. Plan: appendectomy, alcohol withdrawal protocol with lorazepam, thiamine and folate supplementation, continue levothyroxine, addiction medicine consultation prior to discharge.

Internal medicine clinic. 57-year-old male for follow-up of coronary artery disease. He has chronic stable angina, exertional chest discomfort relieved by rest, ongoing for two years. Stress test previously demonstrated inducible ischemia; he remains on aspirin, metoprolol, and isosorbide mononitrate. Fasting lipid panel today: total cholesterol 248, LDL 172, triglycerides 210, HDL 38 — poorly controlled hyperlipidemia despite atorvastatin 40 mg; will intensify to 80 mg. BMI today 29.4, weight up 6 lb since last visit; counseled on diet and exercise for overweight status. Plan: repeat lipids in 3 months, cardiac follow-up, lifestyle counseling referral.

Inpatient note: 44-year-old male admitted with acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. CT pulmonary angiography shows a segmental pulmonary embolism; started on heparin transition to apixaban. History of COPD on maintenance tiotropium with prior exacerbations; current admission shows wheezing and increased work of breathing, treated with bronchodilators and a short steroid course. Admission labs reveal hemoglobin 9.8 with normal MCV and iron studies not consistent with deficiency; evaluated by hematology as an unspecified anemia, workup including hemoglobin electrophoresis and reticulocytes pending. Exam: tachypneic, diminished breath sounds with expiratory wheeze, no leg swelling on duplex. Plan: anticoagulation, pulmonary monitoring given embolism and COPD, repeat CBC, and hematology follow-up for anemia classification after discharge.

Neurology clinic. 53-year-old female with epilepsy, well controlled on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily; no seizures in 14 months, reports occasional auras only. She describes months of excessive, hard-to-control worry across multiple domains, restlessness, muscle tension, and poor sleep consistent with generalized anxiety disorder, plus episodic abrupt surges of palpitations, trembling, and fear of dying lasting minutes — panic attacks occurring several times monthly. No seizure activity captured during these episodes per event diary. Started on sertraline with gradual titration and referred for cognitive behavioral therapy. Plan: continue antiepileptic unchanged, EEG not indicated at this time, follow-up in 6 weeks to assess anxiety symptoms and medication tolerability.

Urgent care. 23-year-old male with five days of facial pressure over the maxillary area, purulent nasal discharge, nasal congestion, and post-nasal drip, worse when bending forward. No fever today, mild cough. Exam: tympanic membranes normal, turbinate edema with yellow-green discharge, tenderness to palpation over both maxillary sinuses, oropharynx clear. Findings consistent with acute bacterial sinusitis given duration and purulent presentation. Plan: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg BID for 10 days, saline nasal irrigation, intranasal fluticasone, analgesics as needed. Return if symptoms worsen or fail to improve within 72 hours.

49M presented to ED with 90 minutes of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to left arm, diaphoresis. Known essential hypertension, on lisinopril 20 mg daily but poorly controlled at home. ECG showed ST elevations in leads II, III, aVF — inferior STEMI. Emergent cath: 100% occlusion of right coronary artery, aspiration thrombectomy and drug-eluting stent placed; also mild disease in LAD managed medically. Troponin peaked at 45,000. Post-PCI course uncomplicated, BP now 138/84 on lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin 80 mg, and dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and ticagrelor. Diagnosis: acute myocardial infarction on background of chronic hypertension. Cardiac rehab referral, echo to assess wall motion, follow-up in cardiology clinic in 2 weeks.

Pediatric clinic: 18-year-old male with 3 days of watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, nausea, and low-grade fever after a cookout; stool studies sent, no blood in stool, exam shows mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs. Impression: acute infectious gastroenteritis/colitis — oral rehydration, bland diet, symptom-guided care. He also has longstanding rheumatoid arthritis, polyarticular and seropositive, on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and folic acid; joints currently quiet, labs stable, continue regimen with rheumatology follow-up. Additionally, he reports worsening worry, restlessness, and two recent panic attacks at school; consistent with generalized anxiety with panic attacks — started on sertraline 25 mg daily with counseling referral. Return if diarrhea worsens or dehydration develops.

Cardiology clinic. 48-year-old male with several months of fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, and constipation; TSH 14.2 with low free T4, consistent with hypothyroidism — started levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. He also reports progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower-extremity edema. Exam: elevated JVP, bibasilar crackles, S3 gallop, 2+ pitting edema. BNP markedly elevated; echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction of 30% with dilated left ventricle, consistent with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Started on lisinopril, carvedilol, and furosemide; counseled on daily weights and sodium restriction. Thyroid replacement may improve cardiac function. Plan: repeat TSH in 6 weeks, cardiology follow-up with repeat echo in 3 months.

Dermatology clinic. 59-year-old female presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the extensor surfaces of both elbows, the knees, and the scalp, present for months with intermittent itching. Nail exam shows mild pitting. Examination and distribution consistent with psoriasis; no joint pain or stiffness reported to suggest psoriatic arthropathy. Started on a high-potency topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily to plaques and a coal tar shampoo for the scalp, with emphasis on moisturizers and avoiding skin trauma. Plan: reassess in 8 weeks; if inadequate response, consider phototherapy referral. Counseled on the chronic relapsing nature of the condition.

Emergency department. 18-year-old male presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain, plus three days of expanding erythema, warmth, and tenderness of the right calf with a red streak tracking proximally up the medial leg. Triage BP 158/102, repeat 154/98 — newly elevated, no prior history. CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrates a filling defect in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery. Lower extremity ultrasound shows no compressible clot; leg findings consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis. Started on IV heparin drip and IV cefazolin. Blood pressure to be rechecked; no antihypertensive initiated in ED. Admitted to medicine ward for anticoagulation, antibiotics, and BP monitoring. Hematology consulted regarding hypercoagulable workup.

Orthopedic clinic. 48-year-old female evaluated for six weeks of low back pain radiating to the buttocks, worse with lifting and prolonged sitting, no neurologic deficits. Exam: paraspinal tenderness in the lumbar region, limited forward flexion, negative straight leg raise bilaterally, normal reflexes and strength in lower extremities. X-ray lumbar spine shows mild degenerative changes only. Assessment: mechanical dorsalgia, muscular strain. Plan: NSAIDs as needed, heat, activity modification, home exercise program, and physical therapy referral for core strengthening. No red flags. Re-evaluate in 6 weeks if not improving.

Endocrinology clinic. 56-year-old female with two months of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, 8-pound weight loss, and anxiety. Exam: fine tremor, warm moist skin, mild tachycardia at 104. Labs: TSH <0.01, free T4 elevated, consistent with thyrotoxicosis. Plan: start methimazole 10 mg daily with beta-blockade for symptoms, endocrine labs in six weeks, thyroid uptake imaging if Graves disease confirmation needed. She also reports a chronic pruritic, erythematous rash on her flexural forearms and neck with lichenification, consistent with eczema; topical triamcinolone ointment prescribed and fragrance-free moisturizers advised, with dermatology referral if refractory.

Inpatient ward note. 61-year-old male admitted with spreading redness, swelling, and warmth of the left lower leg with red streaking up toward the groin, fever, and tenderness for two days, consistent with cellulitis with acute lymphangitis; started on IV cefazolin with leg elevation and marking of erythema borders. He also carries a history of asthma, currently on fluticasone-salmeterol with albuterol as needed; mild wheezing noted on exam, nebs given. During admission he described two months of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, appetite loss, and passive feelings of hopelessness; PHQ-9 score 18, consistent with major depressive disorder, single episode. Additionally reports chronic midline lower back pain without radiculopathy; imaging shows degenerative changes only, managed with heat, stretching, and acetaminophen. Plan: continue antibiotics, start sertraline 50 mg daily with psychiatry consult, pulmonary to review asthma control, and physical therapy consult for dorsalgia.

Internal medicine clinic. 89-year-old male for follow-up of hypothyroidism, likely secondary to amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction. Complains of fatigue, cold intolerance, mild constipation. Labs: TSH 14.2, free T4 low. Also carries asthma with intermittent wheezing and shortness of breath, currently using albuterol PRN with good response, no recent exacerbations. Exam: coarse skin, bradycardic at 54, lungs with rare expiratory wheeze. Plan: start levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, recheck thyroid panel in 6 weeks; continue albuterol inhaler, asthma action plan reviewed; annual spirometry scheduled.

Orthopedic clinic. 78-year-old male with bilateral knee pain, worse with weight-bearing and stairs, morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Exam: crepitus of both knees, varus alignment, reduced flexion, joint-line tenderness without warmth or effusion; radiographs show medial compartment narrowing and osteophytes — bilateral knee osteoarthritis. He also has long-standing calf pain on walking, relieved by rest, with diminished dorsalis pedis pulses and an ankle-brachial index of 0.7 on the right, consistent with peripheral arterial disease; already on aspirin and atorvastatin, advised graded walking program. Knee management: acetaminophen, quadriceps strengthening, physiotherapy referral, cane use; intra-articular steroid injection offered for the right knee. Plan: follow-up in 3 months or sooner if rest pain develops.

Cardiology ward. 78-year-old male transferred with 2 hours of crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm, diaphoresis. ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF; troponin 14.2 — acute inferior wall myocardial infarction. Taken emergently for catheterization; PCI of the right coronary artery with a drug-eluting stent; started on dual antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statin. He also reports bilateral knee pain, worse with weight-bearing and stairs, with crepitus and joint-space narrowing on X-ray — osteoarthritis of both knees. Plan: cardiology monitoring, cardiac rehab referral, acetaminophen for knee arthritis, avoid NSAIDs, orthopedics follow-up.

Urgent care visit. 51-year-old male with two days of sore throat, painful swallowing, and low-grade fever. Exam: pharyngeal erythema with exudate, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, absent cough; rapid strep positive. Diagnosed with acute streptococcal pharyngitis, treated with penicillin VK for 10 days. He also reports recurrent episodes of sudden, exquisite pain at the right first metatarsophalangeal joint; today the joint is warm, swollen, and exquisitely tender, typical of an acute gout flare. Serum uric acid previously elevated at 8.9. Started colchicine for the flare, counseled on low-purine diet and hydration; consider allopurinol initiation after flare resolves. Plan: follow-up in 2 weeks.

ED note: 24-year-old female presents with 18 hours of periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, nausea, temperature 38.2 C, tenderness with guarding at McBurney's point, Rovsing sign positive; CT abdomen shows acute appendicitis, scheduled for laparoscopic appendectomy. Of note, she carries a diagnosis of chronic kidney disease with baseline creatinine 1.8, eGFR 42 — perioperative hydration planned, contrast avoided. She also has documented benign prostatic hyperplasia with obstructive urinary symptoms on tamsulosin, continue home dose perioperatively. NPO, IV fluids, ceftriaxone and metronidazole preoperatively, surgery consulted, admitted to surgical ward.
